#623. Scientists tracked kids for 8 years. What they found about screen time was surprising

An eight-year study of children in Finland has revealed a surprising connection between screen time and brain function. Researchers found that children who spent more time using screens tended to have better cognitive processing abilities as teenagers, challenging the widespread assumption that screen time is necessarily harmful to developing brains.

The findings suggest that the amount of time children spend in front of screens may be less important than how they use that time. Activities that encourage learning, creativity, and problem-solving could be particularly valuable. Researchers emphasize that the goal should not be to eliminate screen time, but to balance it with physical activity and mentally stimulating experiences.

The discovery comes amid growing concerns about insufficient physical activity among teenagers. A sedentary lifestyle has been linked to poorer academic performance, while regular exercise is known to support brain function, particularly in adults. However, scientists still have much to learn about how physical activity, sitting, and screen use during childhood influence thinking abilities later in adolescence.

These questions are especially important because childhood and adolescence are critical periods of brain development. Changes in attention, memory, and learning during these years can have lasting consequences, potentially influencing educational opportunities and career paths well into adulthood.

To investigate these relationships, Finnish researchers examined how screen time, physical activity, and sedentary behavior from childhood through adolescence were associated with cognitive performance in teenagers. They also explored whether the connections differed between boys and girls and whether the intensity of physical activity made a difference.

More Screen Time Linked to Better Thinking Skills

One of the study's most unexpected findings was that greater screen time throughout childhood was associated with better cognitive processing in adolescence.

Cognitive processing refers to the mental abilities people use to take in information, pay attention, remember details, learn new things, and solve problems. These abilities play an important role in school performance and everyday decision-making.

The findings challenge the idea that all screen time should be viewed as harmful. However, the researchers caution that the relationship may depend on what children are actually doing while using digital devices. Watching videos, playing games that require strategic thinking, and engaging in educational activities may involve very different levels of mental effort.

"The findings suggest that screen time can support children's and adolescents' cognitive processing. Presumably, the essential point here is what kind of things they do in their screen time. Teachers and parents should encourage children to use devices and screens in such ways that promote active thinking, problem-solving, creativity, and learning," states Doctoral Researcher Petri Jalanko from the University of Jyväskylä.

"We should not regard screen time solely as harmful but seek balance between physical activity and screen time that promotes active thinking," Jalanko summarizes.

Exercise Affects Boys' and Girls' Brains Differently

The researchers also uncovered a more complicated picture of how physical activity relates to thinking and memory.

Among girls, spending more time engaged in light-intensity physical activity since childhood was associated with better working memory during adolescence. For boys, greater participation in guided physical activity over the same period was linked to stronger working memory.

Working memory is the brain's ability to temporarily hold and use information. It allows someone to remember instructions while completing a task, keep track of numbers during mental calculations, or follow a conversation while processing new information.

Light-intensity physical activity generally includes relatively gentle movements that do not substantially increase breathing or heart rate. Guided physical activity refers to exercise carried out with some form of instruction or supervision, such as organized sports or structured exercise sessions.

The differences between boys and girls suggest that the relationship between exercise and brain health may depend on more than simply how much a person moves. The type of activity, how it is organized, and the individual's sex could all play a role.

Another Surprising Finding About Physical Activity

The study produced another counterintuitive result. Teenagers who reported spending less time in unsupervised physical activity tended to perform better on measures of cognitive processing.

Yet when researchers used wearable sensors to objectively measure movement and heart rate, they found no association between overall physical activity or sedentary time and cognitive performance.

One possible explanation is that wearable devices measure movement without revealing what a person is actually doing. For example, a sensor may record periods of sitting or physical activity, but it cannot determine whether someone is solving a difficult problem, studying, participating in an organized activity, or simply resting.

This distinction could help explain why questionnaire responses revealed relationships that were not apparent in the sensor measurements.

"Our study indicates that the connections of physical activity and sedentary behavior to cognitive processing are complex and depend on the sex, the type and assessment method of physical activity and sedentary time. Moreover, boys and girls may benefit from different types of physical activity in view of brain health," Jalanko adds.

"However, we need more intervention studies to find out causal relations and sex differences in this respect. Moreover, it is important to examine more specifically the effects of the intensity of physical activity on changes taking place in cognitive processing."

The findings come from an eight-year follow-up conducted as part of the PANIC study, a long-running Finnish research project investigating children's physical activity and nutrition.

The current analysis included 260 participants, consisting of 124 girls and 136 boys. Their average age at the adolescent assessment was 15.8 years.

Researchers collected information about physical activity and sedentary behavior using both questionnaires and wearable devices that combined heart rate monitoring with movement measurements. This approach allowed them to compare participants' reported activities with data collected by sensors.

To evaluate cognitive abilities, the researchers used the CogState test battery, a collection of computerized assessments designed to measure aspects of mental performance. The tests examined learning, attention, and working memory.

Importantly, the findings show associations rather than cause and effect. They do not establish that increasing screen time will improve a child's thinking abilities or that reducing certain types of exercise will produce cognitive benefits. Intervention studies, in which researchers deliberately change participants' activities and measure the results, are needed to determine whether these relationships are causal.

Nevertheless, the results offer an important perspective on the continuing debate over children's screen use. Rather than treating all time spent with digital devices as equally harmful, the researchers suggest paying closer attention to whether those activities encourage active thinking and learning.

The research also highlights the importance of considering different forms of physical activity rather than focusing exclusively on the total amount of exercise children receive.

Together, the findings suggest that supporting healthy brain development may require a more nuanced approach, one that combines physical activity with opportunities for learning, creativity, and mental engagement, including those that take place on screens.

The study was published in the scientific journal Pediatric Exercise Science.

#622. Klopp and Wirtz offer glimpse of bright German future

Germany's fall from grace in recent years has seen the team drift away from the fans. But Monday's drubbing of the Netherlands and the impact of Jürgen Klopp, Florian Wirtz and emerging youngsters offers hope.

"Extraordinary," "Insane," "Magnificent," "A special group." Even by Jürgen Klopp's effusive standards, Germany's 5-0 win over rivals the Netherlands on Monday was clearly pleasing.

Despite a patchy start to his reign, Klopp's relentless positivity towards a group of Germany players not viewed in the most flattering light outside the squad has been rewarded.

"Everyone will go home with a smile on their face, and for at least the next three or four months, no one will be questioning the German national team," Klopp told German public broadcaster ARD, referencing that Germany will not play again until the end of March 2027.

"Instead, they'll be thinking: 'This could really turn into something. We have wonderful footballers, great characters," Klopp said, and added: "The lads are even surprising themselves."

The former Liverpool and Borussia Dortmund coach took the job in July after Julian Nagelsmann paid the price for another German early World Cup exit, this time to Paraguay in the last 32. Klopp always preached patience, particularly after his first two matches yielded a fortunate 1-1 draw with the Netherlands and a 1-0 home loss to Greece.

It paid off on Monday as Germany performed with the hallmarks of Klopp's great club sides — fierce pressing, intensity, pace and a measure of joy. Perhaps it is in Florian Wirtz that Klopp's impact is more notable.

The 23-year-old has struggled to make a significant impact at Liverpool since moving to the Premier League from Bayer Leverkusen at the beginning of last season. But he has four goals in his last four games for Germany and is demonstrating the ability that earned him a €125 million ($137.5 million) move to England.

"I only knew him from television. I was shocked when I saw him on the pitch for the first time. An extraordinary footballer," Klopp said after the Netherlands match.

"We've also found the right position for Flo. It helps that he's so vocal. He's the first pressing player, he can press two players without getting tired."

That quality was evident in Wirtz's first goal on Monday, when he won back possession on the edge of the Dutch box before combining some dazzling footwork with a brilliant, curled finish.

But Wirtz wasn't the only attacking bright spot for Germany. Rookie wingers Derry Scherhant and Brajan Gruda both scored and were a huge threat throughout. Klopp gave debuts to both earlier this year as he sought to spread opportunities. The pair have offered Germany a pace they often lacked under Naglesmann and his predecessor Hansi Flick.

"They can both play, my goodness," said Klopp.

Scherhant, who opened the scoring with another stunning strike, spent many days of his boyhood on the terraces of the Olympiastadion in Berlin, where Monday's game was played. Unlike many pros, he bounced about Berlin's lower league clubs as a youth before Hertha Berlin signed him up. He then moved to Freiburg in 2025 and is rapidly emerging as a player who can implement Klopp's style and reflect the coach's attitude.

"A few years ago, people told me I wouldn't make it as a pro. Then I became a pro. And even then, some people still said it wasn't enough—that the Regionalliga (Germany's fourth tier) was the best I could hope for,” Scherhant said.

"It's just unbelievable that I get to stand here now with the satisfaction of having proven those people wrong."

Proving people wrong is also a major part of Klopp's remit. After failing to get beyond the quarterfinal of a major tournament since 2016, the German public's interest in and enthusiasm for its men's national team had waned. Klopp's mission he said, was to "to prove to Germany and the world that we can play soccer."

While that was achieved on Monday, the loss (and subsequent 0-0 draw) against Greece in the Nations League game were evidence that it won't all be plain sailing. Indeed, Germany have had plenty of false dawns of late, as captain Joshua Kimmich alluded to.

"We've been through a tough time," he said. "A clear victory doesn't make all that go away," he added before saying that the task was to "turn potential into quality and a team that's all about 'what ifs' into a team that's all about 'reality.' That's the art of it."

Klopp too, for all his hype, was keen not to get too far ahead of himself.

"We want to gradually solidify it. We're not done yet. We still have a few areas to work on. But I'm looking forward to our future — it's crazy what's still to come," he said.

In Nations League terms, that will be a matchup with world champions Spain, or Portugal or Belgium before qualifying for Euro 2028 begins. For now though, Klopp and his players can enjoy some time with those smiles on their faces.

The Himalayas tower below the clouds, capped in icy snow in new snapshots captured from aboard the International Space Station.

Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk was looking out one of the windows aboard the space station when the most incredible view came into focus  — and thankfully he had a camera handy and was able to capture these striking scenes of the Himalayas from space.

Above the mountain range, fluffy clouds hang in the atmosphere. Below, the expansive Himalayas are covered in bright snow and ice, which looks somehow both white and blue at the same time as the bright sunlight streaks across the breathtaking expanse.

This frosty winter scene showcases the mountain range from orbit, from about 250 miles (400 kilometers) above Earth's surface. But even from this distance, the magnitude of this mountain range is palpable. The Himalayas stretch across five different countries including Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan. And the Himalayas include some of the highest mountain peaks on planet Earth, including Mount Everest.

Himalayas 🗻 https://t.co/IzGzu20H4QNovember 17, 2026

From orbit around Earth, you might expect even the largest landmarks on our planet to appear miniscule. But somehow, in these photographs snapped by Kutryk during NASA's SpaceX Crew-13 mission, even from hundreds of miles above our planet you can really see and feel the immense scale of this mammoth mountain range.

It's unclear exactly where above the mountain range these photographs were taken, but it is always amazing to think that within these sweeping landscapes are people living their lives, likely unaware that an astronaut is taking in the beauty of their home.

Perhaps somewhere hidden under the clouds in one of Kutryk's photographs are hikers climbing up the side of Mt. Everest, completing their own bucket list adventure as the astronauts watching from above complete theirs.

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. #620. Inside the ‘Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic’: A Recipe for Blending Brands With TV (and a Full-Circle Career Moment for Host Drew Barrymore)

The folks behind CBS‘ Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic are hoping to make this holiday special an annual Thanksgiving week tradition.

“I feel like this is going to become part of our cultural tradition,” says Scott Weintrob, founder of Studio Large Eyes and executive producer of the special. “Every Thanksgiving for the next 10 years, with the Pillsbury Bake-Off as the trigger to Thanksgiving week.”

The show is actually a collaboration between CBS and General Mills — which, incidentally, owns the “Bake-Off” trademark in the United States. (“Which is why they cannot call The Great British Bake Off the Bake Off in the U.S. and they have to call it The Great British Baking Show,” says Lisa Balzo, head of brand studio partnerships at General Mills.) Related Stories TV 'Survivor 51' Star Lewis Kelly on His $1 Million Coin Flip and Joining the Cast at the Last Minute TV CBS Inks New Deal to Air Kennedy Center Honors

In developing the special, Weintrob drew on his background in advertising, which has included award-winning work with Rihanna (he designed and directed Amazon’s Emmy-winning Savage x Fenty show) along with Lewis Hamilton x Ferris Bueller’s Day Off, reimagining the film’s classic valet scene with Lewis Hamilton, Edward Norton and Ferrari, which went viral. (He also recently directed and produced Mr. T: I Pity the Fool for Netflix and created Orlando Bloom: To the Edge for Peacock.)

Weintrob’s company, Studio Large Eyes, aims to create brand-inspired entertainment with the philosophy “entertainment first, marketing second.” He says his background crossing both advertising and TV gives him a unique perspective to understand both parties and what their objectives are. “They are quite different,” he says. “And they have different approaches. Being able to talk to networks and streamers and also being able to talk to global brands. I had this in-between knowledge because they are different in so many ways but they all are trying to do the same thing, so I was perfectly positioned to be the conduit.”

Balzo notes that GM, parent company of Pillsbury, had been interested in the idea of a “big grand spectacle” that would incorporate one of the company’s brands. She had already met Weintrob previously at an industry event, and the two began having conversations about some options. “I started talking [with Weintrob] about the history of the Bake-Off, and how it used to be this kind of big grand spectacle that was put on as a live event,” she says. “Over the years, we’ve done various different things with it, and it’s become a smaller digital activation. We’ve also collaborated with the Food Network. I mentioned to Scott that we have been talking about, for years, wanting to bring it back to its full glory. And he pitched this incredible live event.”

“What I originally said to them was, I love the format of the Westminster Dog Show as a baking show, a large event as a live, two-hour special focusing on ordinary people doing extraordinary things,” Weintrob recalls. They agreed on the idea and decided that Thanksgiving would be a key time for the project to air. “I felt we had the opportunity to go and talk to distributors about making this wonderful event. And that’s the key word: It’s an event.”

Balzo says the concept “felt so perfect” and “felt very serendipitous to me at the time. He had this project in his head that that was so perfectly aligned with Pillsbury and what we were looking to do with the Bake Off.”

Back to that trademark: Pillsbury held its first Bake-Off in 1949, when it was called Pillsbury’s Best Grand National Baking Contest. A total of 100 finalists went to New York to compete, and each received at least $100 and kept the G.E. stove they baked on. Eleanor Roosevelt presented the grand prizes, which ranged from $25,000 to $50,000.

Balzo says that baking competitions are immensely watchable because it offers inspiration for viewers at home. “The recipes they’re making are so relatable, and I think people are really going to feel that when they’re watching” the new show, she said, adding that many brands are trying to get into this space, and for GM, the Bake-Off special offers an “authentic connection” with Pillsbury. “It feels like bringing back something that people have already experienced and want more of, as opposed to trying to advertise through content like this.”

For 2026’s Bake-Off, Weintrob began assembling a production team and then setting up meetings with distributors. “When network TV is involved, the word ‘spectacle’ is a brilliant word as a reference point,” he shares. “It needs to be a spectacle to work on network, and CBS saw just how great the show could be. They were the perfect partner to work with.”

Balzo agrees. She cites Barrymore’s authenticity and relatability as two qualities that make her a great host. “Drew authentically remembers that experience [of the commercial], and the brand means something to her,” Balzo says. “She really cares about that connection and the authenticity to the brand in this partnership, and I think people will see that come through on screen when they watch the special, which is why we’re so excited to have her as our host. [In addition], we wanted this to be about more than just baking. We want to tell the stories of a diverse set of people and their backstories and what baking means to them and memories mean to them. And she’s the perfect host to pull those stories out of our contestants. It was incredible to watch her on set because it felt like she was having just this intimate conversation with [the bakers]. I think they felt that too.”

Weintrob and showrunner Brielle Cohen watched 250 submissions from home bakers to cull the list down to 24 competitors who all have “incredible” backstories to share. In addition, famed baker and author Amirah Kassem will join Barrymore and celebrity chef judges Christina Tosi and Dook Chase in the special. It was filmed live on Oct. 23, he shares, which meant a tight turnaround for the Nov. 23 airdate.

For her part, Balzo says this was the first time General Mills had done anything “on this scale,” so they really leaned on Weintrob and the production team to guide them through the process, though GM did play a hand in everything from creative direction to final casting to set direction to the judges and host. Execs also saw all the cuts and provided feedback. (Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic is produced by Studio Large Eyes, Pantheon Media Group and Juma Entertainment. Executive producers include Weintrob for Studio Large Eyes, Jennifer O’Connell, Ariel Brozell, Eden Sutley and Martha Chaput for Pantheon, Robert Horowitz for Juma Entertainment and Brielle Cohen is showrunner. Balzo, Kenzie Caron and Eleanor Harkness serve as executive producers for Pillsbury.)

But, he adds, it’s not just matching a brand with a network and assuming the magic will happen. He says there is a lot of listening on his end and working with the brand to understand what they need while at the same time creating something that’s right for a distributor and their audience. “You’ve got to create bespoke entertainment for a brand,” he summarizes. “You can’t just send them random ideas.”

There’s also the challenge of the promotional timeline for brands vs. distributors. Brands usually begin working on their promotional campaigns months out, while the distributors work on a shorter timeline, sometimes even just weeks. Weintrob says he worked with both companies to come up with an approach that benefited each of them.

Both Weintrob and Balzo hope this special becomes an annual tradition that families can enjoy for years. And, Weintrob suggests, the special could expand to include Valentine’s Day or Super Bowl editions, for example.

“As a brand and especially the Pillsbury brand, the whole family is so important,” Balzo adds. “So we wanted to make sure that we created something that could be one of those moments to bring families together around and create memories around.”

Pillsbury Bake-Off Classic airs Nov. 23 from 8-10 p.m. ET/PT on CBS and streams on Paramount+ (Premium).

"A space-based capability such as this could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by countries and companies around the world."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Last month, the U.S. Defense Intelligence Agency (DIA) released a chilling and info-packed report judging the scope and breadth of threats posed by the nation's adversaries in space.

The new report focuses on China, Russia and the emerging space powers of Iran and North Korea. It looks at what's happening in Earth orbit and beyond, including cislunar space, the region between our planet and the moon.

The report — the 2026 edition of "Challenges to Security in Space" — is the third iteration of the DIA's unclassified intelligence assessment on space-related challenges and threats to U.S. national security, as well as the extent to which space is treated internationally as a warfighting domain.

Information within the report, which you can read here, is current as of July 2026. DIA's mission is to provide intelligence on foreign militaries to help prevent wars, and win the ones that are fought.

The report's up-front finding is that China, Russia, Iran, and North Korea are developing, testing, deploying and using space capabilities "in a way that threatens the security of all space systems and their associated space benefits."

Indeed, China and Russia are developing "a formidable spectrum" of offensive capabilities to degrade or destroy space services of other countries, from kinetic destruction to sophisticated jamming and cyber operations.

The DIA report also notes that "the production of cheaper, smaller, and simpler satellites, which are faster to develop and deploy, along with the expansion of commercially available launch services, are driving the rapid integration of commercial space alternatives to support national security."

While space commercialization is making previously government-centered space services widely available to interested parties, the DIA report adds, that availability also includes state and non-state actors with malign interests.

A major item dealt with by the DIA is "counterspace" — and it's not the kind that you'll find in your kitchen.

Counterspace operations can be either offensive or defensive. They can be used on purpose to reversibly or irreversibly deny, disrupt, degrade, damage or destroy a space object or component of a space system.

Here are the key elements of counterspace, as identified within the DIA report:

The DIA report underscores that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon.

Russia is doing so despite its obligation to comply with the 1967 Outer Space Treaty. That U.N. agreement prohibits the placement of any objects carrying nuclear weapons, or any other kinds of weapons of mass destruction, into orbit around Earth.

"A space-based capability such as this could cause rapid and sudden loss or degradation of thousands of satellites operated by countries and companies around the world," the DIA report states, "as well as to the vital communications, navigation, scientific, meteorological, commercial and national security services they provide."

A nuclear detonation in space could be tailored to impact satellites in most orbits, the DIA report warns, from low Earth orbit for commercial and reconnaissance satellites, geosynchronous orbit for critical communications, and medium Earth orbit for navigation and timing satellites.

The newly issued DIA report also observes that exploring cislunar space is of increasing interest to spacefaring nations for potential scientific and economic opportunities. However, nations such as China "may be exploring military applications from cislunar space," the report notes.

China has stated its goal of developing a cislunar space economy by 2045.

"China is also the first country to attempt sustained operations on the far side of the moon, with numerous projects slated to support that effort through the next decade. China portrays its interest in cislunar space as peaceful, but PRC [People's Republic of China] officials have also discussed pursuing military capabilities in cislunar space," the report states.

Placing a keen eye on the DIA report is Peter Garretson, a senior fellow in defense studies at the American Foreign Policy Council and a strategy consultant who focuses on space and defense.

According to Garretson, the most significant positive change from earlier DIA appraisals is the explicit assessment that Russia is developing a satellite designed to carry a nuclear weapon. He told Space.com that the DIA's expanded treatment of the threat of a nuclear weapon on orbit reflects concerns in the Congress and the Trump White House.

However, Garretson also flagged what he said is a consequential omission in the report: the disappearance of the prior treatment (in the 2022 version of the report) of research competition, surveillance beyond geosynchronous Earth orbit and the potential military use of deep space for staging reserve forces.

In Garretson's view, the DIA needs to help put the puzzle pieces together for Congress and the attentive public about what exactly China is doing, and how it fits together in the nation's strategy to achieve comprehensive space dominance.

According to Garretson, "everything they are doing, from launch cadence, reusable launch, commercial space investment, investments in power, propulsion, repair, manufacturing, to commercial assets working together" supports both an economic expansion toward new resources and what China hopes will be overwhelming military power and strategic depth.

Garretson senses the moves by China to develop extractive and in-space industries "is truly the strategic threat that could crush American space power. Now is the time to be making the investments to ensure we have a 'freedom's forge' and 'arsenal of democracy' in space that can protect the open space commerce that is the nation's strategy."

As for the DIA's outlook for the future: The agency concluded that space almost certainly will remain an increasingly competitive and crowded environment as space capabilities improve and other countries seize opportunities in the final frontier.

"The increase of Chinese, Russian, Iranian and North Korean counterspace capabilities, rapid growth in the number of space objects, and the proliferation of requirements for space-enabled services," the DIA report states, "will all complicate operations in space in the coming decade."

Leonard David is an award-winning space journalist who has been reporting on space activities for more than 50 years. He also wrote "Mars: Our Future on the Red Planet" released in 2016 by National Geographic. Leonard  has served as a correspondent for SpaceNews, Scientific American and Aerospace America for the AIAA. He has received many awards, including the first Ordway Award for Sustained Excellence in Spaceflight History in 2015 at the AAS Wernher von Braun Memorial Symposium. #618. Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

Brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism showed remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies

To explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies."

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

People with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

This increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research

The results raise important questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?"

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support."

The researchers now plan to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.

Materials provided by Society for Neuroscience. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#617. How Iran’s Pegah Ahangarani Turned Her Family Archives Into a Regime-Challenging Oscar Hopeful

The director of 'Rehearsals for a Revolution,' the U.K.'s submission for best international feature at the Academy Awards, on 40 years of Iranian history told through her own life — and how an exile built the film with almost no money.

“Cinema is not just part of my life,” begins Pegah Ahangarani. “It’s me, actually.”

The director and actress grew up on film sets. Both of her parents were filmmakers themselves and immersed their children in the Iranian entertainment industry. Ahangarani became a child star, skyrocketing to fame at just 14 in 1999’s The Girl in the Sneakers. “I won a lot of awards,” she smiles to The Hollywood Reporter. But even she couldn’t have predicted the award-winning success of her debut feature-length documentary, Rehearsals for a Revolution. Related Stories Movies Record Number of International and Animated Features Oscar-Eligible This Season Music Don Toliver Postpones O2 Arena Show After Evacuation Due to "Unknown Substance" Released at Manchester Concert

The Cannes-premiering — and L’Œil d’or-winning — project is a poignant reminder of the power of memory. Ahangarani, whose other essay documentaries include shorts I Am Trying to Remember (2021), My Father (2023) and Child Soldier (2024), sketches her entire life story in this latest work. Drawing from personal archives, home videos, street protest footage, newspapers and recorded voices, she retraces more than 40 years of Iran’s turbulent history. From the late ’70s up until the war with the U.S. and Israel, Ahangarani pieces together and narrates intimate recollections from her life — the vanilla scent of her schoolteacher’s hair and desperate search for her uncle in videos from the 1999 Iranian student protests among them — that help to form the portrait of a country shaped by political repression, and in constant hope for a revolution.

Personal is the operative word in this co-production between the Czech Republic and Spain. “I want to tell my audience: ‘Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility,'” says its director. As daunting as that task was — Ahangarani has already been arrested and spent time in the notorious Evin Prison, and expects not to be able to return to Iran at the risk of a lengthy jail sentence following the release of this film — she remains steadfast in her belief that using family archives is the greatest weapon at her disposal against the regime. “I realized, ‘Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools,'” says Ahangarani. “Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe.”

Having left Iran in 2022, Ahangarani shares candid reflections with viewers about the guilt she’s experienced in the wake of this year’s civilian massacres and brutal crackdown on the Woman, Life, Freedom movement back home. From London, where she has been settled since 2023, Ahangarani talks to THR about putting that guilt up on screen — and being selected as the U.K.’s submission for best international feature film at the 2027 Oscars: “When you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land… [Now], there is one place that accepted me.”

You grew up in film and TV. You were a child star. But when did you first realize you’d like to direct films yourself?

I grew up in cinema, yes. All of the crew members were like my family members. I called them aunties and uncles. (Laughs.) I cannot separate myself from cinema. Cinema is not just part of my life — it’s me, actually. I started cinema as my main career when I was 14. I acted in one film, The Girl in the Sneakers, and that film became very successful. I won a lot of awards. I was a teenager, and I was super happy. And then a few years after that, I remember I saw some documentaries and I thought, “OK, I’d like to maybe be a documentary filmmaker.” I made a few documentaries, but they were very naive. It [was] TV-style documentaries. Then I got familiar with [the] essay style in literature, and then I started exploring that style in some documentaries. I saw some Chris Marker documentaries for example, and Jonas Mekas.

I thought maybe I should find that style for myself, so six or seven years ago I made a short documentary with this style. I used personal archives and I used my voiceover as a narration, and I started making very personal documentaries. That film became very successful as well. The New Yorker published that documentary. It premiered at IDFA Film Festival and a lot of festivals after that. And then I made another short documentary, same style, and another one again. And then after those three documentaries, I started making this one.

The archive of film and photos you use in this is just incredible. Is it daunting, or were you nervous, crafting an entire project around such intimate artefacts and stories?

Yes, actually. (Laughs.) I had a lot of concern about it, and not just for this film. […] A few years ago, when I was living in Iran, I went to my grandmother’s house, and I found some old family albums there. And I started looking through the photographs, and then I saw one photo. My mom was there. My father was there. I was there too. I was two or three years old, and I noticed a man who was standing next to my father, but his face had been scratched out. And I asked my grandmother, “Who is this person? Why has his face been scratched out?” She said, “He was your father’s best friend. He was executed after the revolution because he was a political prisoner.” And I realized my grandmother didn’t destroy the whole photo. She kept that photo, just scratched that face. After that shocking moment, I realized that maybe my responsibility as a documentary filmmaker is to find these old family photos, this personal footage, and find these scratched-out faces and bring them back to life, bring them back to the frame, and bring them back to our collective memory.

After that, I thought a lot about these archives, and I realized, ‘Okay, these are my materials, these are my tools.’ Because I think these personal archives can stand against the dictatorship, the official version of history that the dictators want us to believe. From that day, I started thinking about how I should use these materials as my facts. […] If you go deeper [into] one photograph, if you focus on it, you can see the part of our history in that photograph. But that wasn’t easy at all. When I made that short documentary, I sent it to my mother because my mother was one of the characters, my father was one of the characters, and I had a lot of concern because they might be in trouble after that film. But they were okay. I remember one thing: I sent my film to my grandmother, and I told her, “Okay, I made a short documentary based on the photo that you kept for me.” And she said, “Yes, maybe I kept that photo just for you to make this documentary.”

This is a co-production between Spain and the Czech Republic, is that right? What work went into getting this over the line? Because using your own photos, films and narration, it strikes me as incredibly inexpensive documentary.

[It was made] with nothing, actually. (Laughs.) I had a producer [with whom] I made three of my short documentaries, Kaveh Farnam [founder of the Czech Republic’s Media Nest], and he’s an Iranian independent film [producer] outside of Iran. I remember when I was making a previous documentary, I found him, I texted him, and he joined the project. And that one was like this — I didn’t need money because I worked with my personal archives. But I wanted support for distribution [and] things. At that time, I was inside Iran, and I told Mr. Farnum that after this film, if I got arrested or something like that, please publish the film. I needed someone just for publishing. And then when I moved to London, I talked to Mr. Farnum about this feature film, and he said, “Okay, I’m in,” and I didn’t need any money for that. I just needed a small [amount of] money for my editor [Arash Ashtiani]. The Spain company [Fasten Films]… they found me and they wanted me to make another film for them. And then I told them, “I have one film, it’s finished now. I can send it to you, and if you want, you can join this project as well.” Right after they watched the film, they texted me and they told me, “Oh, we love the film. We want to join the project.”

They supported us because we needed some money for the copyright of the music and sound design, and they have a good relationship with a French distributor… Then they sent the film to the Cannes Film Festival, and they have a very good relationship with Cannes because they are French, and everything actually happened after that. But for the process of making this, we didn’t need any money.

One standout part of the documentary, for me, is when you’re scrolling through some of those harrowing images and videos from this year’s protests and you talk about your guilt and trying to compensate for that with the film. What has it been like reckoning with that through these glamorous film festivals?

Everything was very strange because right after the massacre, we were in the process of editing episode five. We wanted to show me [and] my new life as an immigrant, living in exile, and then war happened and massacre happened, and so we didn’t know how we should respond [to] these disasters in our film. That was a very complicated situation because I couldn’t focus on the film. I told my editor, “Cinema doesn’t mean [anything] anymore after all these dead bodies.” And then I realized that, “Okay, I should share all these concerns with my audience because this is the only way I should tell them.”

But I didn’t have any idea that the the film [could] be successful. During the process of making this, it was just me and my editor, Arash, and a little mic, and a very intimate space. I remember the distribution company texted me and told me the director of Cannes, Thierry Frémaux, told us maybe you can be in the official selection. That was very exciting. That day, I just lay down on the sofa in our office… I couldn’t handle this much excitement. We realized we can compete with, for example, Steven Soderbergh, because he had a film in Cannes in the official documentary selection. And in Cannes, they told us, “You won the best documentary prize,” and I think I’m in the middle of some dream or something like that. Not because my film is successful now, but because I try to show these 40 years of Iranian history and this ongoing struggle of the Iranian people, and everybody around the world now can see this struggle.

What do you hope audiences are talking and thinking about after seeing this film?

After the first screening in Cannes, I realized one thing, which was very sweet: When the film finished and people started clapping, many of them came and told me, “We think we love your people as much as you.” I thought, ‘So this is cinema.’ You can show something that people don’t have any idea about, and they can resonate with it, and they can feel this struggle. They can feel [for] your people, which is amazing.

Many people, after watching the film, they think they know me very well [and that] they’re a friend of mine, which is very sweet. I think the film is successful because I could create a sense of intimacy. Through the narration and through the film, I want to tell my audience: “Come and sit with me. I want to share everything with you, even my fragility.”

This film is officially the U.K.’s official Oscar submission for best international feature. What does that mean to you?

That was great news. Not just because of the film, but when you leave your country, you think you are kind of stateless. You need somewhere to attach. You need a place. You need a land. When I left Iran, I thought, “OK, this is just a temporary situation.” And then I realized that no, maybe it’s permanent. I cannot go back anymore. I should accept my new life, and that was very difficult. When the U.K. announced that they picked our film … I had a feeling like I wasn’t stateless anymore. There is one place that accepted me.

I’m sure you miss your family so much, but you don’t envision a future where you can return?

When I left Iran in 2021, I didn’t have any plan to stay outside of Iran. I left my country with just one carry-on to participate in the IDFA Film Festival for my short documentary. And after the second screening, my mother, she was in Iran [and] called me and told me the regime had called her and asked her to interrogate me about the film. She told me, “Stay outside for a while, for one or two months.” And then the “Woman, Life, Freedom” movement happened and I published a video to show my solidarity with that movement, and then my mother told me they sent a letter [saying] there is a court order against me. They seized my apartment and my bank accounts in Iran and I realized that I can’t go back. If I go back, I have to go to jail. I was in jail for one month in solitary [confinement], but if I go back, maybe I could be in jail for six or seven years or something like that. I decided to stay outside because I wanted to make my film.

A biblical mystery, an ancient Egyptian inscription and a "ring of fire" solar eclipse 3,200 years ago hold clues to when Ramesses the Great ruled.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The solar system is a clock that can be run in both directions. On Aug. 2, 2027, that clock will bring the moon's dark central shadow — a path of totality — back to Egypt. A total solar eclipse will sweep across the country, passing directly over Luxor and plunging some of ancient Egypt's greatest surviving monuments into darkness. Totality will begin in Luxor at approximately 1:02 p.m. EEST and last 6 minutes 22 seconds, according to Time and Date.

We know when it will happen because we can calculate the motions of Earth and the moon centuries in advance. But run the same celestial clock backward and eclipses become one of nature's most precise timestamps.

Astronomers can reconstruct where the moon's shadow fell thousands of years ago, even when nobody left a record of it. When an ancient text reliably describes an eclipse, it can anchor a moment in history to a specific place and time.

We know from astronomical calculations that eclipses crossed Egypt long before anyone left an identifiable written record of one. On April 1, 2471 B.C., a total solar eclipse swept across northern Egypt during the age of the great pyramid builders. In research published in 2025, archaeoastronomer Giulio Magli at the Polytechnic University of Milan proposed that the eclipse may help explain why Pharaoh Shepseskaf broke with tradition and built a huge rectangular tomb at South Saqqara instead of a pyramid. It's a tantalizing hypothesis, but no surviving Egyptian text records the eclipse.

Astronomers can calculate that an eclipse happened, but using it as a historical timestamp requires evidence that someone actually saw it and recorded it. That's where an eclipse almost 1,300 years later becomes particularly intriguing.

A passage in the Old Testament book of Joshua describes the sun and moon as if they stopped in the sky. After leading the people of Israel into Canaan — modern-day Israel and Palestine — Joshua prayed: "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon. And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies." Ancient Gibeon is about six miles (10 kilometers) northwest of Jerusalem.

In research published in 2017, researchers Colin Humphreys and Graeme Waddington at Cambridge University in the U.K. claimed it could refer to an annular solar eclipse on Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. It's a controversial interpretation, not least because it depends on exactly how the ancient Hebrew text is translated. However, if correct, it could be the oldest recorded solar eclipse with a date that has been identified — and it could also more accurately date the reign of Ramesses II. Also known as Ramesses the Great, he reigned for 66 years during Egypt's New Kingdom, commissioned Abu Simbel, made major additions to Karnak and Luxor Temple, and lived to be over 90. His reign marked the final peak of ancient Egyptian imperial power. According to the BBC, he is the "Jupiter" of the pharaonic system. However, the precise dates of his reign remain subject to debate, with historians using a combination of archaeological, historical and astronomical evidence to reconstruct the chronology.

Now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, the Merneptah Stele is a large inscribed granite monument written in the fifth year of Pharaoh Merneptah's reign, successor to Ramesses II. Discovered in 1896 at Merneptah's mortuary temple on the west bank of the Nile, opposite modern-day Luxor, it describes an Egyptian military campaign in Canaan and mentions Israelites. Egyptologists generally date Merneptah's reign to around 1213 — 1203 B.C., placing his fifth year around 1209/1208 B.C. That means the Israelites were already living in Canaan by then.

Using calculations that accounted for changes in Earth's rotation over thousands of years, Humphreys and Waddington identified an annular eclipse visible from Canaan for five minutes on the afternoon of Oct. 30, 1207 B.C. If the biblical passage does describe this event, that's a fixed astronomical date that could be used to refine the chronology of the Egyptian pharaohs. The researchers proposed that it occurred during the second, third or fourth year of Merneptah's reign.

If Humphreys and Waddington's interpretation of the biblical text is correct, the eclipse of 1207 B.C. could be the oldest solar eclipse identified in a written record. The researchers propose that Ramesses II reigned from approximately 1276 to 1210, with an uncertainty of about a year, slightly different from the conventional dates of 1279-1213 B.C. used by the British Museum.

So an eclipse can be like a timestamp on an undated photograph, but this one does not show that the book of Joshua actually describes an eclipse. The interpretation of the Hebrew has been challenged by Marinus Anthony van der Sluijs, whose paper argues that the biblical narrative states that the sun was standing over Gibeon and the moon was over the Valley of Aijalon simultaneously — so not an eclipse at all.

On Aug. 2, 2027, there will be no such ambiguity. We already know where the moon's shadow will cross Egypt, when it will reach Luxor and how long darkness will last. Almost 4,500 years separate that eclipse from the one that crossed Egypt in 2471 B.C. and 3,233 years from 1207 B.C., but both are movements of the same celestial clock. Run it forwards, and it predicts the future. Run it backward, and occasionally an eclipse of the sun can put a date on history.

#615. Amanda Seyfried, Robert De Niro and Timothee Chalamet to Host ‘SNL’ in December

Here are all of season 52's hosts and musical guests.

After leading the New York Knicks to their first NBA championship in more than half a century, Jalen Brunson will add another accomplishment to his career highlights this fall: Saturday Night Live host.

Brunson is set to host the Sept. 26 season premiere of SNL and will be joined by musical guest KATSEYE. He’s the first athlete to host the show in more than three years (Travis Kelce was the most recent one, in March 2023) and the first active NBA player to take center stage at studio 8H since LeBron James back in 2007.

Dakota Johnson (Oct. 3) and Shane Gillis (Oct. 10) will each host SNL for the third time in the fall. Johnson will be joined musical guest Turnstile, and Rosalia will be the musical guest for Gillis’ episode. SNL then takes a couple weeks off before returning on Halloween with Obsession breakout Inde Navarrette making her debut as host and musical guest Gracie Abrams. Related Stories TV NBC to Air Princess of Wales Cancer Charity Documentary TV 'The Traitors: New Blood' Renewed for Second Season at NBC

On Nov. 7, comedian and online/social media creator Druski will make his hosting debut (his booking was first reported at Puck). He’s the first person to make the leap from the online creator world to hosting SNL, though Druski has also had several TV, movie and commercial roles and hosted the BET Awards in June. The Strokes will be the musical guest for the episode, the band’s fifth time on the show.

A week later, comedian and former SNL writer John Mulaney will host for the seventh time. Phoebe Bridgers will make her second appearance as musical guest.

The show will close out 2026 with three shows. Amanda Seyfried will host on Dec. 5 with musical guest Don Toliver; it will be the first time for both. On Dec. 12, Robert De Niro hosts for the fourth time, with Slayyyter debuting as the musical guest. Timothee Chalamet hosts the Christmas show on Dec. 19 (also his fourth time), and Charli xcx will make her fourth appearance as the musical guest.

The cast of SNL will be fairly stable — at least compared to the sizable overhaul prior to season 51 last year. Chloe Fineman announced her departure from the show in July after seven seasons, and writer and occasional performer Martin Herlihy left after five seasons. The rest of last season’s cast, however, is returning, and Saidah Belo-Osagie and Grace Reiter are joining the show as featured players.

#614. The hidden language of psychopathy is not what scientists expected

The way people describe their lives may offer surprising clues about their personalities, including traits associated with psychopathy. A new study from the University of Mississippi challenges the familiar image of psychopaths as cold and emotionless, revealing that their patterns of language can be far more complex than expected.

Researchers examined hundreds of personal life stories and discovered that three major traits associated with psychopathy, boldness, meanness, and disinhibition, were connected to distinctly different ways of using words. Some of the findings were particularly unexpected. For example, people who scored higher in meanness tended to use more positive language, while those with greater boldness used fewer words associated with anxiety.

The findings, published in the journal Personality and Individual Differences, suggest that psychopathic traits can influence everyday communication in subtle ways that conventional stereotypes often overlook.

"The goal here is not to diagnose psychopathy based on language," said Ky Bray, an Ole Miss doctoral candidate in psychology. "It's to point to the fact that psychopathy shows up in everyday behaviors, even subtle behaviors like language.

"If we want to understand psychopathy and the different traits that comprise it, we need to think creatively about how these traits shape social interaction."

What 450 Life Stories Revealed About Psychopathy

The researchers used a psychological framework known as the Triarchic Model of Psychopathy, which examines three distinct personality dimensions. Boldness generally involves confidence and fearlessness, meanness reflects tendencies toward callousness and reduced empathy, and disinhibition involves difficulties with impulse control. According to Laura Drislane, an assistant professor of psychology at the University of Mississippi, these characteristics can affect ordinary behaviors, including how people describe their own experiences.

To investigate these connections, Drislane and Bray recruited 450 participants, including college students and individuals who reported having been incarcerated. Each person responded to open questions about important moments in their life, including their greatest highs, lowest points, and major turning points.

After writing their personal accounts, participants completed a questionnaire designed to measure their levels of psychopathic traits. The researchers then analyzed the written responses using specialized software that identifies patterns in word choice.

The analysis focused on how frequently participants used language associated with different psychological categories, including positive and negative emotions, achievement, social influence or clout, and risk. By comparing these language patterns with the personality scores, the team identified several intriguing relationships.

Surprising Differences in Positive and Negative Language

Participants with higher disinhibition scores generally used more negative words in their personal stories. They were also less likely to mention friends or use language connected to positive emotions and personal achievement.

Meanness, however, showed a very different pattern. People scoring higher in this trait tended to use more positive language, along with more words related to achievement and rewards. They also used fewer expressions associated with negative emotions.

Boldness was associated with another distinctive pattern. Participants with higher scores used fewer anxiety-related words, including terms such as fear, afraid, and worry. Their personal accounts also contained fewer references to mental illness.

These differences suggest that psychopathic traits do not produce a single recognizable style of communication. Instead, different characteristics are associated with different ways of describing emotions, goals, relationships, and personal experiences.

"What this tells us is the story we tell about our life has meaning," Drislane said. "It helps people make sense of their experiences, develop a worldview and a coherent sense of who they are.

"What we're starting to see is that in psychopathy, there are traits that relate to differences in meaning-making and the ways people think about their life."

Why Psychopathy Is More Complex Than the Stereotypes

The researchers also discovered that the relationship between personality traits and language changed depending on which question participants were answering. Someone describing a difficult experience, for example, might use language differently than when recalling a personal success.

This variation is important because it challenges the assumption that psychopathy is characterized by consistently flat or emotionally empty communication. Instead, the findings indicate that language patterns depend on both the particular psychopathic trait and the context in which someone is telling their story.

"People tend to think of psychopathy as one thing, but it's actually multidimensional," Bray said. "What we mean when we say that everyone exists on this spectrum. Everyone has some degree of meanness, boldness, and disinhibition.

"Viewing it from a multidimensional perspective allows us to observe how those traits might manifest in nonforensic populations, in people who have not committed a crime. That allows us to see how these traits affect college students, business professionals, or interpersonal relationships."

Like many personality conditions, psychopathy is better understood as a spectrum rather than a simple distinction between people who have it and those who do not. At one extreme is the familiar cultural image of a "psychopath," while people at the opposite end score low in all three dimensions.

This approach allows researchers to examine psychopathic traits throughout the general population, including among people who have never committed a crime. It also helps explain why the same broad label can encompass individuals with very different personalities and behaviors.

How Understanding Psychopathic Traits Could Improve Treatment

Recognizing these differences has implications beyond understanding everyday speech. Researchers have linked dimensions of psychopathy to serious outcomes, including criminal behavior, repeat offending, and intimate partner violence. Examining each trait separately may provide a clearer picture of how these risks develop.

"That's in part why there's a movement away from calling people 'psychopaths,' because we don't view psychopathy as a category," Drislane said. "But psychopathic dimensions can predict important outcomes, things like crime, recidivism, or intimate partner violence.

"What our research, including this paper, suggests is that it's important to look beyond that label and into the different components or dimensions of psychopathy, because each of those dimensions actually has a unique set of outcomes or things that it can predict."

Researchers also emphasize that psychopathy can be treated, with interventions aimed at reducing problematic symptoms and behaviors. Understanding the psychological processes behind boldness, meanness, and disinhibition could help scientists develop more targeted approaches and potentially identify ways to prevent severe problems from emerging.

"If we want to be able to treat or ideally even prevent psychopathy from developing, we need to understand the mechanisms at play," she said. "That comes down to understanding the unique contributors for all three of these dimensions."

Materials provided by University of Mississippi. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#613. Danny Boyle on ‘Ink’ and Murdoch, the ‘Trainspotting’ Toilet Scene and How ‘Slumdog Millionaire’ Almost Went Straight to Video

The Oscar-winning filmmaker spoke with The Hollywood Reporter in front of an audience at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, where he was honored with the Maverick Director Award.

“Decades before clickbait, before Fox News, before OnlyFans, before Truth Social, before Google, before Facebook, before any of it, something started that we’re still living with the consequences of,” Danny Boyle said while recording an episode of The Hollywood Reporter’s Awards Chatter podcast in front of an audience at the recent SCAD Savannah Film Festival, where he was being honored with the fest’s Maverick Director Award. The Oscar-winning director was referring to the fateful 1969 meeting of Australian businessman Rupert Murdoch and British newspaperman Larry Lamb, and the tabloid journalism that it spawned, which is chronicled in Boyle’s latest film, Ink, which Netflix will release in theaters on Dec. 11 and on its streaming platform on Jan. 8. Related Stories SCAD Savannah Film Festival 'American Doctor' Director on Her Powerful Gaza Doc: "I Wanted to Do Something" Movies Ron Howard Wasn't Sure He Was the Right Director for 'Avedon'; This Is What Changed His Mind

The 70-year-old Englishman has directed 15 features over the past 32 years, including 1994’s Shallow Grave, 1996’s Trainspotting, 2002’s 28 Days Later, 2008’s Slumdog Millionaire, 2010’s 127 Hours and 2015’s Steve Jobs. Described by the New York Times as “a cinematic hypnotist” and by The Guardian as “a film director in a class of his own,” he won best director Academy, Golden Globe and BAFTA awards for Slumdog, and an Emmy for his work on the London 2012 Olympic Games Opening Ceremony. And he also was presented with a Britannia Award for Artistic Excellence in 2009 and a BFI Fellowship in 2010.

You can watch the listen to or watch the entire episode above, or read select excerpts below…

On the scene in Trainspotting in which Ewan McGregor swims through “the worst toilet in Scotland”…

“CG was just beginning to emerge in cinemas. In fact, there was a Christmas film out at the time with Tim Allen playing Santa Clause, and they squeezed him into a chimney pot. That’s one of the very first uses of CG in film. It looked terrible, I thought. I thought, ‘We’re not going to do it like that,’ because somebody said, ‘Oh, you could use CG,’ as it was at the time. We wanted to do it live. So we used a theater trick, the trompe l’oeil: you cut the toilet in half and film it from the side. So, obviously, it isn’t a toilet on this side; it’s the slide that McGregor goes down. Then Brian [Tufano, the cinematographer] told Ewan [McGregor, the film’s star] to twist his feet ’round at the end, because then people will think it’s the U-bend that you’re going ’round, which curiously people do. It’s just that illusion that we buy into. If you believe the actors, you’ll believe anything! So people believed it was the worst toilet in Scotland, even though it smelled of chocolate, because all the shit was chocolate, and it was delicious! All the prop girls had candles burning so that everybody felt good about being there all day.”

On how Slumdog Millionaire almost went straight-to-video instead of to the Oscars…

“There was a change of regime at Warner Bros., and there was a change of emphasis. They decided that films that they put a bit of money up for would not be worth the cost of releasing, so they decided to put them straight out on video. And it wasn’t just my film, there was a Guy Ritchie film as well, Revolver, and a couple of others like that, as well. Fortunately, Peter Rice, [who was running Fox Searchlight at the time and] who’s just taken over Netflix, picked it up and bought it off Warners, which normally doesn’t happen. He knew somehow that when you played it with an audience, it would prove itself.”

“The film’s really about truth, so you have to tell the truth about Murdoch and what Murdoch was like. Even though people would prefer you to paint him as a villain, he, in fact, had many reservations about what was going on. But he didn’t act on them, which is as much condemnation as you need, I think, rather than just portraying him as a villain.”

“He is the kind of actor like [Al] Pacino is, who can take you to an impossibly dark place — in Pacino’s case, the ordering of the execution of his brother [in The Godfather, Part II] — and yet you still lean into the character. Jack has that. If you think about he stuff he does in Sinners and in 28 Years Later: The Bone Temple, he’s a monster, and yet you’re drawn into him. That’s a weird duality he has, which not many actors do. He’s a wonderful, wonderful actor.”
