#612. A mysterious twist in the universe’s oldest light could reveal new physics

A mysterious twist in the universe's oldest light could offer clues to physics that scientists have yet to discover. But before researchers can determine whether this subtle signal reveals something extraordinary about the cosmos, they must answer a crucial question: Is the effect actually coming from the universe, or could it be an illusion created by the telescopes observing it?

The mystery centers on the cosmic microwave background (CMB), a faint glow of radiation left over from approximately 380,000 years after the Big Bang. This ancient light provides a remarkable snapshot of the "baby universe" as it existed nearly 13.8 billion years ago, allowing scientists to investigate conditions from the earliest stages of cosmic history.

When the universe was about 380,000 years old, it had cooled enough to become transparent, allowing light to travel freely through space. As radiation scattered off free electrons during this transition, it acquired a small amount of linear polarization. Polarization describes the direction in which light's electric field oscillates, and a similar effect occurs when sunlight scatters through Earth's atmosphere.

Now, observations suggest that the polarization of this ancient radiation may have shifted slightly as the light traveled across the universe. This possible rotation, called cosmic birefringence, is especially intriguing because it could point to physical processes not explained by the Standard Model, the leading theory describing fundamental particles and their interactions. Confirming the effect might even provide new insights into dark matter and dark energy (see Sidebar).

A Mysterious Cosmic Signal or a Telescope Error?

There is a major obstacle to interpreting this potential discovery. An extremely small error in how a telescope's polarization detectors are aligned can produce a signal that looks almost identical to cosmic birefringence.

To help address this problem, physicists at the University of California San Diego developed a new technique for checking how accurately different groups of detectors measure polarization angles. They tested their approach using existing observations collected by the European Space Agency's Planck satellite, which mapped the universe's ancient radiation in extraordinary detail.

The research was led by Postdoctoral Fellow Anto I. Lonappan, Chancellor's Distinguished Professor of Physics Brian Keating, and Associate Professor of Physics Kam Arnold. Their findings were published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

Separating Real Cosmic Effects From Instrument Errors

Previous studies have suggested that the polarization of the CMB may have rotated by just a fraction of a degree over its nearly 14 billion years of travel. Although that sounds insignificant, such a tiny change could have enormous implications for fundamental physics.

Unfortunately, a telescope whose polarization detectors are misaligned by a similarly small angle could produce precisely the same apparent rotation. If every detector shares the same alignment error, the resulting measurements cannot distinguish that error from a genuine rotation of the cosmic signal.

The UC San Diego researchers found a way to investigate the problem from another angle. Rather than relying on a single combined measurement, they compared separate polarization maps generated by different groups of detectors.

If cosmic birefringence is real, its effect should appear consistently across all these maps. By comparing the maps with one another, the researchers can effectively eliminate any rotation shared by all of them. What remains reveals differences in the calibration of the individual detector groups, making it possible to identify inconsistencies that might otherwise complicate the search for new physics.

"The signal we are looking for is incredibly small, so we have to be certain that we are seeing the universe and not our instrument," said Lonappan. "Our method gives us a complementary way to check that distinction. Before interpreting a tiny rotation as new physics, we want to know that the calibration itself can be trusted."

Testing the Mystery With Planck Satellite Data

To evaluate their technique, the researchers analyzed eight polarization maps produced using Planck observations. They then compared their findings with results from an established approach called the Minami-Komatsu analysis, which is used to distinguish instrumental rotation from possible cosmic birefringence.

Although the two methods rely on different assumptions, they produced consistent results. This agreement provides an important independent check on how relative detector calibration errors are being assessed.

The new approach also has a deliberate limitation. Because it removes any rotation common to all the maps, it cannot independently measure the overall polarization angle or determine how much the universe itself may have rotated the light. Establishing that absolute rotation still requires an independent reference for calibrating the overall angle.

To demonstrate how their findings fit with existing measurements, the researchers combined their reconstruction of relative calibration differences with the common calibration value inferred from the established analysis. This produced an estimated cosmic birefringence angle of 0.37 ± 0.12 degrees, matching the Minami-Komatsu result.

Importantly, this agreement does not independently confirm that the ancient light has actually rotated. Instead, it shows that the new method can reproduce results from the existing framework while providing a separate way to examine potential calibration problems.

Searching for Gravitational Waves From the Early Universe

The technique could also play an important role in another major pursuit in cosmology: the search for gravitational waves generated during the universe's earliest moments.

To understand why, scientists distinguish between two patterns of polarization in the cosmic microwave background, known as E modes and B modes.

E modes were first detected in 2002. They arise from density variations in the early universe and form symmetric polarization patterns. B modes have a different appearance, featuring patterns that resemble curls or swirls.

One known source of B modes is gravitational lensing, which occurs when the gravity of matter between Earth and the early universe bends and distorts the path of ancient light. Scientists have already observed B modes created through this process.

However, researchers are also searching for a different kind of B mode that could have been produced by primordial gravitational waves. These ripples in spacetime may have originated during an extremely early period of rapid cosmic expansion, known as inflation. The distinctive B mode signal associated with those primordial gravitational waves has not yet been detected.

Finding it would provide powerful evidence about gravitational waves in the early universe and could offer strong support for particular models of cosmic inflation, potentially transforming scientists' understanding of how the universe began.

Why Extremely Precise Measurements Matter

The challenge is that even a slight error in a telescope's polarization calibration can cause some of the much stronger E-mode signal to appear incorrectly as B modes. This contamination could make an instrumental artifact look like an exciting cosmological discovery.

The UC San Diego method could help prevent such mistakes by identifying differences in polarization angle calibration among detector groups. That makes it a potentially valuable tool for future experiments searching for the extremely faint signatures of primordial gravitational waves.

This kind of independent verification will become increasingly important as observatories develop the ability to measure cosmic polarization with greater precision. One example is the Simons Observatory, where Keating serves as principal investigator.

As these instruments become more sensitive, researchers will need equally rigorous methods for confirming that the faint signals they detect are genuine features of the universe rather than imperfections in their equipment.

"The detection of primordial B modes would transform our understanding of the early universe, so the measurement must survive rigorous calibration checks," said Keating. "Anto has developed a useful new framework for testing relative polarization-angle calibration. This is ultimately about knowing when we can trust a measurement."

Beyond the Standard Model: Dark Matter and Dark Energy

The possibility of cosmic birefringence is particularly fascinating because it could reveal physics that lies beyond the Standard Model.

Although this framework has been remarkably successful at describing fundamental particles and their interactions, it cannot explain everything in the universe. Among its most important unanswered questions are the identity of dark matter and the origin and observed magnitude of dark energy. Together, these mysterious components account for approximately 95% of the universe's total energy density.

One possible explanation for cosmic birefringence involves a hypothetical field associated with particles resembling axions. Such a field could interact with light and gradually alter its polarization as it crosses the universe. However, these particles have not been confirmed to exist, and they would not necessarily be responsible for dark matter.

Other theoretical explanations connect the possible rotation to fields associated with dark energy, the mysterious phenomenon linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe.

If cosmic birefringence is eventually confirmed, it could provide an entirely new way to investigate these cosmic mysteries and reveal evidence of physical laws beyond those currently understood.

For now, the first challenge is ensuring that the subtle signal can be trusted. By giving researchers another way to identify potential measurement errors, the new technique strengthens the foundation for future discoveries that could reshape our picture of the universe.

Aldebaran looks for all the world like the brightest member of the Hyades star cluster. It isn't — and discovering why changes the way you look at constellations.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For years I looked at Taurus and saw something perfectly sensible. There was the Hyades, the big V-shaped cluster that forms the bull's face, with Aldebaran, noticeably brighter and more orange than the other stars, the dominant star. Every diagram reinforced the arrangement — Aldebaran was the eye of Taurus, the Hyades made the face, and in my head they became one object.

Then I discovered that Aldebaran has nothing to do with the Hyades. I remember going outside afterward and looking again, half expecting the deception to become obvious now that I knew. It didn't. Aldebaran still looked completely at home among the other stars. The difference is hidden in the one dimension our eyes judge poorly when we look into space — depth. Aldebaran is about 65 light-years away, while the Hyades are roughly 150 light-years distant. The orange eye of Taurus is a foreground star that happens to lie almost exactly along our line of sight toward the Hyades.

This fact exposes one of the most convincing tricks in stargazing. The night sky looks flat, and our brains are extremely willing to believe it. But it has incredible depth — and when you can see parts of the night sky in 3D, that's when you begin to appreciate that you're not looking at a flat map. Instead, you begin to see our cosmic neighborhood as it really is. By appreciating depth, you learn its geography.

Taurus is now easy to find from the Northern Hemisphere during the evening. Once it's dark, look east for a small, tight knot of stars — the Pleiades open cluster (M45) — and then look nearby for a much larger V-shaped arrangement. That V is the Hyades, with unmistakably orange Aldebaran apparently sitting on one arm. Aldebaran's name is derived from the Arabic Al Dabarān, meaning "the follower," because it appears to trail the Pleiades across the night sky.

The Hyades is a real physical group of stars — an open cluster — that formed together and moves through our galaxy together. About 153 light-years away, the Hyades is the nearest open star cluster to Earth. The name means "the rainmakers" because their rising and setting times in the ancient Greek sky coincided with wet weather. The stars in the Hyades are of a similar age — and mostly sun-like stars, or similar — so astronomers can tell that they all formed together in the same nebula.

Orange-red star Aldebaran — the 14th-brightest star in the night sky — is the interloper, sitting less than half as far away from the sun. If you could somehow view the neighborhood from another part of the Milky Way, the familiar arrangement would fall apart. Aldebaran would no longer sit conveniently in the bull's face, and Taurus itself would stop looking like a bull.

Constellations aren't objects in the same sense as a planet or star cluster. They are merely views. Even stars that appear almost side by side can be separated by enormous distances. Our entire view of the night sky is a line-of-sight, 2D phenomenon — so all the patterns we see are an illusion.

Start with Aldebaran and the Hyades using only unaided eyes. Once you have the V, remind yourself of the distances — roughly 65 light-years for Aldebaran and 150 for the Hyades — and try to imagine pulling the orange star toward you while leaving the rest of the cluster behind. Stargazing like this can be much harder than it sounds. Even the brains of seasoned stargazers are hard-wired to find patterns of stars — constellations — and they rarely practice seeing stars at their correct distances.

Binoculars are worth using for the Hyades because the cluster is broad, so low magnification suits it well. Binoculars show many additional stars, but that's not really the point. Knowing what you're looking at changes the observation more than magnification does.

Trying to see the night sky in 3D is best done one constellation at a time, but I warn you — it makes you suspicious of everything. Next time you trace Orion, Cassiopeia or Auriga, you'll always be wondering which stars are nearby and which merely look that way. Looking up the distances and working it all out for yourself is an eye-opening experience.

Learning constellations gets you around the sky in a basic sense, but learning how to dismantle them and put them back together is when you begin to know the night sky as it really is.

This week is dominated by the moon. The moon is already waxing when the week begins and becomes the full Beaver Moon — a supermoon — on Nov. 24. That means progressively brighter evening skies and increasingly poor conditions for faint galaxies, nebulae and other low-contrast objects. Aldebaran and the main Hyades stars are bright enough to see from suburban skies even under strong moonlight, so you don't need to travel somewhere properly dark. Swapping your view from 2D to 3D takes only a little imagination. However, that could change in the few nights around the full moon — particularly on Nov. 23, when the waxing gibbous moon will move close to the nearby Pleiades, its strong light reducing the number of faint stars visible around them. Use binoculars to find some of its hundreds of stars.

I'm a stargazer and not at all interested in Greek mythology, but it sometimes helps to know a few basic ancient myths when finding constellations. A good example is the constellation Cepheus. It's named after a king of Ethiopia, husband of Cassiopeia and father of Andromeda — all three of which are close by in the northern sky right now. Look west after dark, away from the bright moon, to find the Summer Triangle — Vega, Deneb and Altair — which by now is sinking into the west. From Deneb, look north for a distinctive five-star pattern resembling a child's drawing of a house, with a square base and pointed roof. That's Cepheus. Its brightest star is Alderamin, about 49 light-years away, which marks one corner of the "house."

#610. Even Sienna Miller Was Surprised by That ‘War’ Ending

The female lead of the HBO/Sky legal drama's first season, who is no stranger to weathering tabloid scrutiny herself, opens up to THR about who came out on top in the high-profile divorce in the end.

[This story contains MAJOR spoilers from the War finale.]

Sienna Miller doesn’t quite know why she keeps getting tapped to play women caught up in the public eye. Since breaking out two decades ago as Edie Sedgwick in Factory Girl, the American-born English actress has made a speciality out of portraying women navigating intense media scrutiny — from Alfred Hitchcock’s tormented muse Tippi Hedren in The Girl to the embattled political wives of Showtime’s The Loudest Voice and Netflix’s Anatomy of a Scandal.

“I think it’s less that I’m seeking out these roles and more that those are the roles that people see me as, probably because a famous actress is part of my identity in a way [but] I don’t feel is part of me,” Miller tells The Hollywood Reporter on a recent video call from her home in the U.K. “I feel like an actor who’s not very famous — and a mom. But it’s quite funny to perhaps send myself up by playing heightened versions of whatever I imagine people might assume that to be.” Related Stories TV All's Fair in Love and 'War': Creator George Kay Explains His Ruling on Morgan and Carla's Divorce TV Archie Renaux on 'War's Resident -- and Misunderstood -- Bad Boy

Miller’s latest TV role is no exception. In creator George Kay’s HBO/Sky legal anthology drama War, which just aired its finale on Thursday in the U.S., Miller plays film star Clara Duval, whose messy, high-profile divorce from Dominic West’s billionaire tech founder Morgan Henderson becomes a feeding frenzy for both the press and their ruthless legal teams. At the center of the dispute is an equitable split of Zephyr — the ostensibly “less toxic” social media platform that Morgan built after watching Carla endure relentless online bullying and that Carla named after Mary Darby Robinson’s poem “Ode to the Muse.”

Though their lawyers push them toward scorched-earth tactics to win at all costs, the pair ultimately choose to settle on their own terms, resulting in a surprisingly optimistic portrait of life after separation. “I think the normalizing of divorce is something that should be more commonplace in the world. It doesn’t have to be hell,” Miller says. “I thought that the ending was very poignant and sweet.”

In the wide-ranging chat below, Miller opens up to THR about shedding her own people-pleasing tendencies to play a “narcissistic” (but surprisingly sympathetic) actress, why she thinks Carla really came out on top in the divorce — and how she reflects now on her own experience of being tabloid fodder in her 20s: “I’m more in a kind of anthropological way interested in it [now], because I feel maybe from some PTSD that I am separate from it.”

War creator George Kay has said he wanted an actual movie star to play Carla, but he very intentionally did not want to let any of your own personal experiences influence the writing of the character. In hindsight, what did you find most appealing about embodying someone in an esoteric world that you already know so intimately yourself?

I signed on before I knew what it was, because I only read the pilot, so I was learning on the job very much with this. This isn’t a limited series, but for me, it was. [Writer’s note: Kay confirmed to THR that each season of War will center on a new legal dispute, with the parties being represented by the same group of lawyers at rival London firms Cathcarts & Sons and Taylor & Byrne.]

Sometimes when you do a limited series, you have all eight episodes and you can kind of map something out. But with this, I wouldn’t find out till a few days before we’d start shooting the next block [when] we’d get scripts. So it wasn’t that I made a choice to play somebody in those circumstances, and I don’t know now that I need to do it again. But while I was in it and learning who she was as we were going along, I thought it was interesting to feel like somebody very different in those somewhat familiar circumstances. But I think Carla’s much more steely and less naive than I am.

I wouldn’t want to describe Carla as a narcissist, but she certainly comes across as a little high-strung and self-centered.

Where do you think her narcissistic nature comes from? Did you establish any kind of backstory that could shed light on what makes her tick?

I think she’s an insecure woman who has had to deal with underestimation, and I don’t think there was one inciting incident. I think you are either one of two personality types — you either have more of a narcissistic personality, or you’re more of an empathetic person. I, as myself, would walk into a room and be concerned or pretty much aware of everybody within that room, and roughly have a temperature gauge on all of them. With Carla, I think she has decided that she’s the most important person in that room, and she doesn’t feel the need to check in with others. I think she channeled whatever abandonment she experienced into that way of being as a defense mechanism, versus my equivalent — which is exhausting, but is also a defense mechanism.

[Playing] that was really fun. Once I made that decision to be like, “She’s not concerned with other people’s feelings or energies, and she’s very much orbiting herself” — it was so uncomfortable at first to be that way. And then anytime I stumbled upon something that my instinct would be to correct, I was like, “No, she wouldn’t bother her.” And then it was quite a liberating choice.

George has also talked about how you brought an unexpected softness to Carla that was not always part of his original conception of the character. Were there any particular moments in the season that you wanted to soften her a little bit or make her more likeable? Did you ever push back on some of her actions or decisions?

I didn’t feel like I needed to make her more likable. I sometimes needed reasons for the decisions about how she was [acting]. I felt like I really pushed back against the kind of hysterical breakdown on the talk show [in episode five], although people really enjoyed that, because I just didn’t want it to fall into any kind of “hysterical woman” trope situation. I didn’t want Morgan to appear reasonable and Carla to appear unhinged, but that’s often the way the world sees these relationships and sees the dynamics between a couple. If she’s ambitious or if she’s ruthless, she’s a bitch; if he is [those same things], he’s a great businessman. I think it does kick up some of those tropes, which I was really trying to push back on until I realized, “Well, maybe it’s a great mirror to see how women are treated and judged.” Obviously, it gets rectified, and she wins that particular battle.

But there were moments in this that I was trying to advocate for her to be more vulnerable, or more soft, or just more three-dimensional. But then if I didn’t find it, I would just lean into her being really unashamedly a bitch or whatever she is. The moment where she couldn’t remember her son’s age — I was like, “That’s a huge thing [to forget]!” And we were learning this as we were going on. I’m like, “Does she not know her son’s age?” And then I would talk to other cast [members] who were like, “Actually, it’s kind of funny. Just do it.” But I was trying to fight for her a bit in moments.

Even though you and Dominic play the leads of this season, your characters don’t actually spend a lot of time together because they’re always busy strategizing with their own lawyers. What did all of the brief glimpses of Carla and Morgan — in the back of a limousine, in an elevator, in the back alley of the courthouse waiting for their cars in the rain — reveal to you about the nature of their relationship?

I think the thing that Carla and Morgan were missing was time together, and time and energy spent on each other. When they’re forced into those situations, other than the car at the very beginning, I think they realized that there was so much there that was probably salvageable or that they cared about. And once you get into a war situation and it’s you versus them, it’s very easy to forget those moments, the good things. But I think what probably comes across in those poignant moments is a sense of love buried underneath all of it, or consideration at least, or some form of emotion, which I think the lawyers are very good at hiding from you.

Carla’s relationship with Morgan is also very much shaped by their own financial circumstances — he is now a billionaire tech founder, and she has been experiencing a lull in her acting career and a significant dip in her income.

I think through the process of divorce and how acrimonious that is and how savage it is, you can either really sink into the resentment and the loathing, or you can remember what it was that brought you together. In the cross-examination [during the last two episodes], we’re talking about moments when we first met. Parts of it are quite therapeutic for them.

I think she genuinely feels entitled to something for Zephyr. I think she really does feel like she contributed more than he is allowing to be let on to the formation of that company, but she’s just vengeful. I don’t even know that it was ever about the money. I think she was just unhappy and he was unhappy, and then it got ugly. She kind of made it ugly, but that’s because she was convinced he cheated. It’s a whole mess, but there are threads within it that I also struggle to follow. So I put it down to just them being erratic and love not being a linear thing.

Carla and Morgan clearly could have settled their divorce at any point during mediation or arbitration, but it’s not until the end of their two-day trial that they decide to reach a fair settlement on their own terms without any outside intervention. In their last scene together, the two of them share a lovely moment on the beach in Normandy, and they are last seen walking back to her cottage to have a hot chocolate with Gabe (Aran Murphy, son of Cilian), Carla’s son from a previous relationship. What did you make of the resolution of their relationship?

I think they’re both battle-weary by that point, and they’ve seen all of the duplicity amongst the legal teams, and that side of things is so ugly. They’ve humiliated each other publicly and been backed into corners, and I think they don’t recognize themselves in some of those moments. I found I was expecting more fireworks at the ending. (Laughs.) And then in reflection, I think the normalizing of divorce is something that should be more commonplace in the world. It doesn’t have to be hell. I thought that the ending was very poignant and sweet.

Basically, what happened was that Dom and I never really got to work together. So anytime we did, we were very happy, which I think serves the story and adds a little sort of something to the scenes. But I found that scene on the beach touching to shoot and surprisingly emotional. But again, there are so many different ways that this could have gone, and I have to defer to the writing team to come up with the best one. I think Carla should have won! I probably was drawn to it becoming more ugly. But actually, the lawyers are the ugly people, and that’s the moral of the story. Even though Carla and Morgan are also ugly and narcissistic. (Laughs.)

What do you think it says about us as a culture that we immediately think of the worst possible scenario for a high-profile divorce?

Well, I don’t know. I think it’s wealthy people. We want to see them being treated like normal people, being dragged through the mud. It’s the same with Succession. We loved watching those people get it wrong and fall apart. I think there must be some kind of schadenfreude. It’s wonderful to be in those aspirational worlds and then wonderful to be reminded that, irrespective of how aspirational this world is or how great it looks from the outside, they’re two people dealing with shit. It’s just with many more zeros on the end of it.

George has told me his theory about what happens to Carla and Morgan’s relationship, but what do you imagine Carla and Morgan’s lives — either together or apart — will look like going forward?

I think they’ll be really good friends, but I think he will regret [the divorce] more than she will. So that’s me defending my character, and Dom would say the same thing about his. (Laughs.)

Over the last couple of decades, you have played a lot of women — and particularly actresses — who are navigating intense public scrutiny. It’s hard not to think about how the early years of your career in the mid-2000s were overshadowed by British tabloid culture and paparazzi obsession. How do you reflect now on the harsh treatment that you endured in your 20s?

Yeah, it feels so alien to the world that we live in now that it’s almost comical. It’s not comical, but I’m baffled that that existed. The ’90s [had] a lad culture in England, and God forbid, you couldn’t take the piss out of yourself and laugh at yourself. If you couldn’t laugh at yourself or send yourself up, you weren’t worth talking to in England. So I think I kind of absorbed that lad culture and was quite gobby and probably quite fun for them fodder-wise. But the lad culture meant that the paparazzi were just ravenous and unstoppable and aggressive and violent, and it’s just so different to the world [now]. It just would not be allowed; it wouldn’t be tolerated. People on the street wouldn’t stand for it if they saw what was happening.

It was young women that were targeted and cameras up your skirts — just shocking. But you look back and you’re like, “God, that’s not long ago,” and it was absolutely accepted and paid for and devoured. So I’m more in a kind of anthropological way interested in it [now], because I feel maybe from some PTSD that I am separate from it. I can look back on it with curiosity and philosophy versus trauma and just be like, “God, that’s crazy that it wasn’t that long ago, and that’s how we lived.” But pre-social media, in 2008, the whole world shifted. In 2012, it really shifted, but it’s just interesting to look back on that time and to have been such a part of it and feel like it’s so foreign. I think it was too much for anyone to really live like 15 people outside your house and chasing you everywhere you went. I’ve always been the same — I’m quite a normal, grounded person that it just didn’t suit [my life]. I don’t want bodyguards and putting on makeup every day.

You’ve spoken about wanting to take yourself more seriously as an actress, and reaching a point in your life where you are decidedly less interested in hearing other people’s opinions. When did that shift start for you?

I think I always took my work really seriously. I just think it was a battle to be seen as a serious actor in my 20s, but we are way beyond that now. I think when I had my first daughter, life just suddenly felt more serious, and the choices that I was making, they had to be worthy of being away from home and taking my kid on the road, and there was just more levity to each decision. So I feel like the work is something I’ve always taken very seriously, but people didn’t see me as a serious actor until quite a while ago now.

Do you ever worry that playing women who are consistently judged by their image reinforces the narrative you’ve been trying to move past?

It’s interesting. I don’t ever think about that in relation to these actresses. I see them as they should be seen: as people. But I think what I was objecting to is my own personal [experience]. It was a different era of tabloid journalism and scrutiny, and we lived in a monoculture. There weren’t fringe people with opinions on the internet, and it was one media and pretty unanimous news that we were all digesting. So if there was a public persona of you, that was pretty much the [only] public persona of you, and it was very difficult to have a say in that. It’s such a different culture now that I don’t think it exists in the same way. I think that if I was treated the way that I was then, I would have a much louder voice or means to come back at it.

But in terms of [playing] the actresses, I don’t know. I think it’s less that I’m seeking out these roles and more that those are the roles that people see me as, probably because a famous actress is part of my identity in a way [but] I don’t feel is part of me. I feel like an actor who’s not very famous — and a mom. But it’s quite funny to perhaps send myself up by playing heightened versions of whatever I imagine people might assume that to be, maybe. Although I have played a lot of actresses — and I can’t even remember them all now — I’ve also played a lot of non-actresses, so it feels like there’s variety for me.

You and Carla are fundamentally different people, but I would imagine you also know what it feels like to not be able to leave your own house or to live in a gilded cage because of the paparazzi. Even though you have moved past that chapter of your life, do those feelings ever come up when you are playing these women? Or are you always able to separate your own experiences from the characters you play?

No, I feel like when I’m put actually in the circumstances of getting through a pack [of people] into a car, my heart starts racing. I do have some body memory of it, even though I know it’s pretend. That’s your job, I think, as an actor. It’s to summon things or have them just appear for you in this instance because your past experience is what you can draw on. But I think if I was to get another script of a famous actress, I’d probably not do it, unless she was really different.

Unless she was even more awful than Carla?

All episodes of War are now streaming on HBO Max in the U.S. and Sky NOW in the U.K.

#609. Students' List candidates take seats as Serbian parliament opens

Serbia's Student List's candidates have taken their oaths in the inaugural parliament session. As the new majority, they have 90 days to form a government.

Representatives of Serbia's student-led movement were sworn in as lawmakers on Tuesday, just over four weeks after they ended Serbia's strongman leader Aleksandar Vucic's 14 years of rule.

The Students' List candidates officially took their seats in the inaugural parliamentary session as the first step for the youth-backed party toward forming Serbia's new government.

The movement holds 140 seats in the 250-member parliament while Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) holds 103. The remaining seats belong to ethnic minority parties.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Hundreds gathered outside the parliament building in the capital Belgrade, to show their support for the student-backed lawmakers, most of whom are teachers, professors and other professionals with little or no political experience.

Meanwhile, SNS candidates were met with a negative reaction from the crowd. A woman in the crowd poured yogurt over an SNS member's head as she climbed the steps to the parliament entrance.

According to Serbian media, the newly elected lawmakers have been preparing for their first session for days. They will face veteran opposition politicians, including Aleksandar Vucic, who became the opposition leader after his defeat.

The Students' List will have 90 days to name a prime minister, present their programme and form a government, once the parliament is formed.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

The movement unites left- and right-wingers, pro-European and pro-Russian forces. It is focused on making changes in domestic politics and wants to advance European Union accession talks by implementing real reforms. The List opposes sanctions on Russia and the recognition of Kosovo — positions that almost the entire population of Serbia agrees with.

They pledged to improve healthcare, boost education and double the defense budget, along with many other reforms.

The election of a new parliamentary speaker will also lead to the appointment of a new acting president. The speaker has held the role since Vucic resigned in September to run for prime minister.

A snap presidential election must be called by November 27 and held by December 27.

Both parties are expected to put forward presidential candidates, but Vucic cannot seek another term because the constitution limits presidents to two terms in office.

#608. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera has revealed a strange new world

The European Space Agency's (ESA) Hera spacecraft has captured its first close-up image of the Didymos asteroid system, offering scientists a surprising new perspective on the site of NASA's historic asteroid deflection experiment.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos, the smaller of the two asteroids in the system. Hera's latest image provides a look at its larger companion, Didymos, from a side that scientists had not previously seen in such detail.

The image was taken from a distance of 60 km using Hera's monochromatic Asteroid Framing Camera, which captures images in black and white. Although most of Dimorphos, which measures 151 m across, is concealed in shadow, the much larger Didymos, with a diameter of 780 m, is clearly visible.

A Surprisingly Different Side of Asteroid Didymos

"The first thing we said was wow!" observes Hera Principal Investigator Patrick Michel, Director of Research at CNRS / Observatoire de la Côte d'Azur. "This is the other side of Didymos from the one that DART's camera showed us shortly before impact, so this feels like looking at a whole new world.

"This side of Didymos has the same central ridge along its equator that we saw before, but otherwise appears very different, with multiple boulders and craters and what look like patterns of grooves or ridges."

The newly revealed terrain raises intriguing questions about how the asteroid's surface developed and whether NASA's collision with Dimorphos may have left traces on its larger neighbor.

When DART struck Dimorphos, the impact sent material flying into space. Scientists believe some of that debris may have traveled across the roughly 1 km separating the two asteroids and reached Didymos. Determining whether this material contributed to the features now visible on its surface will be an important part of Hera's investigation.

ESA's Hera mission scientist Michael Kueppers adds: "Since we expect a lot of impact-ejected material to have made it across the approximately 1 km of space from Dimorphos to Didymos, it may be that some of these characteristics originate from this transport of material, and we have exciting work ahead of us to sort it out. We look forward to seeing much more of both bodies and systemically mapping all the changes we identify."

NASA's DART Mission Changed an Asteroid's Orbit

Although Dimorphos is largely obscured in Hera's new image, it holds a remarkable place in space exploration history. It became the first object in the Solar System to have its orbit measurably altered by human activity.

NASA achieved this milestone by sending the 580 kg DART spacecraft into Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 km/s. The collision reduced the time the smaller asteroid takes to complete an orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, give or take a minute. That change was substantially greater than scientists had anticipated.

The experiment demonstrated that striking an asteroid with a spacecraft can change its motion through space. This approach, known as kinetic impact deflection, could potentially be used to redirect a dangerous asteroid before it reaches Earth.

Hera Begins Its Investigation of NASA's Asteroid Impact

After a two-year journey, Hera has reached the double asteroid system, located 196.8 million km from Earth. The spacecraft is now preparing for a detailed 'crash site investigation' to examine the consequences of NASA's groundbreaking experiment.

While DART demonstrated that an asteroid's orbit could be changed through a deliberate collision, Hera will help scientists understand the physical processes behind the result. By examining both asteroids and documenting their characteristics, researchers hope to improve their ability to predict how future asteroid deflection attempts might work.

The findings could help transform kinetic impact deflection from a successful one-time demonstration into a dependable, repeatable planetary defense technique. Such a capability could prove critical if an asteroid were ever discovered on a collision course with Earth.

"Seeing this image is a hugely exciting moment for the whole Hera family," comments Hera mission manager Ian Carnelli. "It has taken years of hard work and dedication to reach this point - but we're motivated to know that the adventure is only beginning!"

The mission's next major reveal is scheduled for November 25, when detailed images of both Didymos and Dimorphos will be unveiled, giving scientists and the public a closer look at the asteroids involved in humanity's first successful asteroid deflection experiment.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#607. Trouble at Mars: NASA's Perseverance rover, Odyssey orbiter halt science work due to glitches

Two of NASA's Mars explorers are sidelined by glitches at the moment.

The Perseverance rover and Mars Odyssey orbiter have stood down from science work due to technical problems, NASA announced on Thursday (Nov. 19).

Perseverance has been sidelined by an antenna issue, and the venerable Odyssey is dealing with a balky reaction wheel. NASA hopes both can get back to work at Mars by the end of November.

Perseverance landed inside Mars' Jezero Crater in February 2021, tasked with assessing the area's potential to support past life and with collecting dozens of samples for future return to Earth.

It has done all this and more. The Perseverance team has determined that Jezero hosted a potentially habitable lake billions of years ago. And the car-sized rover has found a wealth of complex organic compounds in Martian rock, some of which might themselves be signs of life (though assessing this hypothesis fully will likely require bringing Perseverance's samples to Earth for analysis, scientists stress).

In addition, Perseverance just set a new distance record for off-Earth driving, rolling past the mark set by its smaller cousin, NASA's Opportunity rover (28.06 miles, or 45.16 kilometers).

Perseverance broke that record on Oct. 11. Just 19 days later, however, the mission team noticed a problem: The rover's main UHF downlink radio — which it uses to send information home to Earth, via data-relay satellites in Mars orbit — failed to send its usual "heartbeat" pings to the main computer.

Perseverance detected this problem autonomously and reacted as it was programmed to do: The six-wheeled robot switched to its backup UHF radio and went into a protective "safe mode," shutting down all non-essential systems.

The rover team recovered Perseverance from safe mode but soon noticed another issue: "The backup UHF radio was transmitting at about half of its expected power output," NASA officials wrote in an update on Thursday.

Perseverance's handlers have stopped using that backup radio as well; the rover is now communicating with Earth directly (without the help of relay orbiters), sending signals to NASA's Deep Space Network dishes via its high-gain antenna.

This pathway features lower data rates, and the mission team wants to prioritize the delivery of diagnostic information. So they've paused Perseverance's science work, which includes observations by its various cameras.

The glitch may be disappointing to devoted Perseverance fans, many of whom have already noticed that the mission website hasn't uploaded any new raw images since Nov. 7. But there's no reason to panic, according to NASA.

"The rover is stable and communicating with the team," agency officials wrote in Thursday's update. "The team is hopeful the rover could return to science by the end of November, and NASA will provide further updates in the future as the team works the issue."

Mars Odyssey's problem may be more serious: The orbiter, which arrived at the Red Planet in October 2001, recently lost the use of one of its reaction wheels.

Odyssey has four reaction wheels, which help the spacecraft maintain its orientation in space. Three of the four must be functional to do this job, and Odyssey already lost a reaction wheel in 2013.

This latest issue cropped up on Nov. 4, when Odyssey went into safe mode. The orbiter stayed in this protective posture until Nov. 6 while mission team members diagnosed and dealt with the problem. They've made some progress, at one point getting the faulty wheel to move when commanded.

"Further testing is being conducted to confirm whether the wheel is recoverable," NASA officials wrote in Thursday's update.

Though it has been out of safe mode for two weeks, Odyssey still has not resumed its science or data-relay work. (The orbiter has long helped NASA's Mars surface craft send information home to Earth.)

"The goal is for Odyssey to return to science and relay operations at the conclusion of these tests and analysis during the last week of November, and NASA will provide future updates on status and timeline as the team learns more," agency officials wrote in the update.

If the reaction wheel, isn't recoverable, Odyssey's days are numbered. The mission team will have to orient the orbiter solely using its thrusters, and Odyssey has enough hydrazine fuel left to do this for a just month or two, according to NASA.

Odyssey's mission has been a rousing success, no matter what happens with the reaction wheel. The orbiter has operated at Mars longer than any other spacecraft, and it has made a number of important scientific contributions.

"Odyssey created the first global maps detailing the composition of the Martian surface, which have become foundational for Mars geologists," NASA officials wrote in Thursday's update.

"The orbiter's surface maps have also played a key role in identifying hazards at landing sites, spotting locations of scientific interest for landers and rovers to explore, and mapping water molecules in the top 3 feet (1 meter) of the surface, including buried ice that could be useful to the first astronauts on Mars."

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He primarily covers human and robotic spaceflight, military space, and exoplanets, but has been known to dabble in the space art beat. His book about the search for alien life, "Out There," was published on Nov. 13, 2018. Before becoming a science writer, Michael worked as a herpetologist and wildlife biologist. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. To find out what his latest project is, you can follow Michael on Twitter.

#606. Chuck Lorre, ‘Grey’s Anatomy’ EP Zoanne Clack, ‘A Different World’ Boss Felicia Pride Join Lineup for SIE Society’s Impact+Profit26 (Exclusive)

In addition, entertainment-education pioneer Miguel Sabido has been tapped to receive the SIE Impact Entertainment Visionaries Award at the Dec. 7-8 conference, which will be held for the first time at USC Annenberg.

The SIE Society (Social Impact Entertainment Society) has unveiled the lineup for Impact+Profit26, its flagship conference “showing that storytellers don’t have to choose between impact and profit.”

TV uber-creator Chuck Lorre, Grey’s Anatomy EP Zoanne Clack and A Different World showrunner Felicia Pride are among those scheduled to take part in the two-day event, which is set for Dec. 7-8.

In addition, entertainment-education pioneer Miguel Sabido has been tapped to receive the SIE Impact Entertainment Visionaries Award at the conference, which will be held for the first time at USC Annenberg, home of the Hollywood, Health & Society, a program of the USC Norman Lear Center. Organizers said the new venue carries special meaning for the field. USC Annenberg’s connection to impact storytelling traces back to the pioneering Soap Summits of the 1990s and early 2000s, which helped spark television’s social impact movement and paved the way for Hollywood, Health & Society.

More than 250 producers, executives, financiers and changemakers are expected to attend the conference, which is presented for the fourth consecutive year in collaboration with the Johns Hopkins Center for Communication Programs.

“Bringing Impact+Profit to USC Annenberg connects us to the history of entertainment education in Hollywood,” said Will Nix, a founder and co-executive director of the SIE Society, whose creative work as a producer includes film, television, theater and digital media productions. “For four years, Johns Hopkins Center for Communication Programs has helped us bring evidence and storytelling into the same room. Impact+Profit is built on partnerships, and we’re grateful to every collaborator who makes it possible.”

Sabido will be honored on Day 1 of the event. The presentation will take place during “The Man Who Proved Stories Can Change the World: A Conversation With Miguel Sabido,” where Sabido will be joined onstage by Robert Rippberger, a founder and co-executive director of the SIE Society, filmmaker and author of The Power of Storytelling: Social Impact Entertainment.

“Long before anyone had a name for this field, Miguel showed the world that a story told with care and purpose could change how millions of people live their lives,” Rippberger said. “His work is the blueprint for what social impact entertainment can achieve. As we celebrate his legacy, we’re also challenging the next generation of storytellers to carry that vision forward with the same courage and rigor.”

The conference will close with “A Conversation With Chuck Lorre,” featuring the Golden Globe-winning writer and producer behind such comedy hits as The Big Bang Theory, Two and a Half Men, Mom, Young Sheldon and Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage. Lorre, who also founded the Chuck Lorre Family Foundation, will sit down with Jay Sures, vice chairman of United Talent Agency, for a closing-night discussion on his career and his philanthropic work.

Additional sessions will focus on AI and social media for measuring impact, reality TV as a force for good, faith and media, the podcast-to-feature pipeline, grassroots impact for independent filmmakers, and a hands-on workshop on designing transitional characters with the Sabido Method.

The Hollywood Reporter is a media sponsor of Impact+Profit26. The event is also supported by First Entertainment Credit Union, NBCUniversal, World Bank Group; media sponsor KCRW; and partners Population Media Center and Schulz Entertainment Law and the UTA Foundation.

Regular tickets are $375 and student tickets are $150 (valid enrollment required). Tickets include two days of panels and workshops, six networking sessions, and food and drink. Registered attendees can use the SIE Society conference app for the agenda, curated networking and badge scanning. Tickets and the full agenda can be found at conference.siesociety.org

The SIE Society is a global community of nearly 1,800 entertainment, corporateand nonprofit professionals, from all storytelling media platforms, who are working at the intersection of storytelling and social change. The SIE Society works to support collaboration and measurable impact across industries through curated programming, thought leadership and year-round engagement.

#605. GTA hasn't gone to space (yet), but these sci-fi games can offer you a life of crime among the stars

Grand Theft Auto 6 is finally out, but if you're a sci-fi aficionado looking for similar experiences set in outer space, there are several alternatives.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

GTA 6 has only just come out, and it's already taken the world by storm and positioned itself as one of the greatest games of all time. Great news for gamers, but what about sci-fi fans?

To this day, Rockstar Games sadly hasn't embraced sci-fi with any of its open-world games (save for those UFO Easter eggs). It doesn't seem likely they'll journey to the stars anytime soon — you can't really do cutting societal satire about space — but that doesn't mean there aren't GTA-adjacent sci-fi adventures set in outer space.

The frustrating thing is that no one has exactly cracked that pitch yet. Non-linear games set in outer space tend to be either too ambitious, like No Man's Sky, or too focused on specific experiences like space combat, like Star Wars: Squadrons.

The end result is a roster of great sandboxes that let us journey to different star systems, but no game that dares to explore a criminal fantasy with the level of depth and opportunities seen in the last few Rockstar games.

With new hardware powering far more complex open-world games, it's only a matter of time before "GTA in space" is a real thing. For now, there are some space games that let us explore sci-fi worlds, roleplaying as criminals and outlaws amongst the stars.

Massive space RPGs like Starfield and The Outer Worlds 2 offer vast playgrounds you can explore and redefine through your actions. The lawful path is the obvious choice if you'd like to save the galaxy, but a life of crime awaits those who tire of the heroics.

Starfield even has a "new game plus" mechanic baked into the player's journey, encouraging experimentation and living different lives, so if you stick with the divisive space RPG, the criminal life is all but unavoidable. And in traditional Bethesda fashion, you're not rushed to the next "main" objective, so if you want to become the most dangerous space criminal in the Settled Systems, you'll be supported by the mechanics and systems. You can always get back to saving the galaxy when you feel like it.

The Outer Worlds 2 is another option if you want to become a star-surfing scoundrel. It might not be as absurdly expansive as Starfield, but Obsidian's whole deal has always been freedom of choice and roleplaying, so you can bet this humorous sequel also lets the protagonist become a bit of an a-hole. The main story already sets you in a collision course with corporate interests, too. Like in Mass Effect and other classic space RPGs, it's your choice to be either a goody-two-shoes or an edgy maniac, and I won't lie: the second option is usually more entertaining.

Last but not least, there's a third game that also has enough going on to support a GTA-inspired fantasy in outer space: No Man's Sky.

It's grown so much over the years that its original space exploration premise has been buried by content like fully customizable space stations, actual cities and towns with alien NPCs, gigantic kaiju-like beasts, and... fishing. The endless free updates have pushed the roleplaying aspects deeper, as Hello Games are really making it the "forever" space game.

Most importantly though, you can be the greatest bad guy the virtually infinite universe has ever seen, controlling entire pirate fleets and firing on (or stealing) every spaceship that you come across. It might be a bit aimless for some, but if you love a "forever game" then NMS can be the biggest space-set criminal sim ever created.

Though it took too long, Star Wars has gotten really close to cracking the GTA formula in outer space in a shameless enough way. 2024's Star Wars Outlaws is, to this date, the closest thing we've received to a space-set sandbox directly inspired by Rockstar's huge hits.

By letting us fully embrace the Han Solo-like scoundrel fantasy, Massive Entertainment delivered a Star Wars adventure that's all about breaking the law. Hell, they even got a wanted system in there that has protagonist Kay Vess dodging stormtroopers and rival criminal factions like you would in Vice City.

Star Wars Outlaws' take on GTA isn't just about the surface-level gameplay and open structure; it also understands much of its playful tone, moral ambiguity, and stressful rhythm. Jumping between several medium-sized maps set on different planets and spaceship sections breaks up the experience a little, so it never quite reaches that level of seamless immersion, but if anyone wants to do a focused version of GTA in space in the future, Massive's attempt is the one game that got at least halfway there.

Before we go (and before you go back to playing GTA VI), we should remember the daring video games that, for a variety of reasons, never got to realize their visions of a crime-oriented space adventure.

Remember Star Wars 1313 and Visceral Games' cancelled project? It's hard not to spot some of their DNA surviving in Outlaws. As Luke Skywalker wisely said before noping out, "No one's ever really gone." Lucasfilm loves that, and it extends to binned video games too, thankfully. Even the elusive Battlefront 3 is back from the dead now.

Bethesda also had something going at some point with "Prey 2", a bounty hunter action game set in a cyberpunk-ish alien world. Before it was canned, it dropped one of the coolest CG game trailers ever made and teased us with a Blade Runner-esque future long before Cyberpunk hit our consoles.

Looking at the future, Ubisoft's Beyond Good & Evil 2 wants to go big and lawless, potentially iterating on Star Wars Outlaws and other open-world crime sims. But years after its announcement and many mind-boggling development news updates, it's hard to believe it's really ever coming out. Maybe the "Before GTA VI" meme can morph into "Before BG&E2" now that Rockstar's masterpiece is finally out.

Ultimately, Rockstar is Rockstar. A one-of-a-kind megastudio with nearly unlimited resources. Trying to replicate GTA does — either on Earth or among the stars — would be an Icarus flight in the making for most studios. There are some GTA-flavored space adventures out there, as we've shown, but we're still waiting for the one. Something that matches the deep storytelling, complete freedom, and cheeky tone of Rockstar's iconic series. OK, I gotta get out of here, I'm too hip for this, I gotta play GTA VI some more.

Jason and Lucia have always known the deck is stacked against them. But when an easy score goes wrong, they find themselves on the darkest side of the sunniest place in America, in the middle of a criminal conspiracy stretching across the state of Leonida — forced to rely on each other more than ever if they want to make it out alive.

Fran Ruiz is our resident Star Wars guy. His hunger for movies and TV series is only matched by his love for video games. He got a BA of English Studies, focusing on English Literature, from the University of Malaga, in Spain, as well as a Master's Degree in English Studies, Multilingual and Intercultural Communication. On top of writing features and other longform articles for Space.com since 2021, he is a frequent collaborator of VG247 and other gaming sites. He also serves as associate editor over at Star Wars News Net and its sister site, Movie News Net.

#604. New discovery reveals what may be holding back room-temperature superconductors

Imagine trains floating above their tracks, energy storage systems that waste almost no electricity, and quantum computers operating with extraordinary efficiency. Superconductivity could help make these technologies possible, but a major challenge has stood in the way for more than a century. Most superconducting materials function only when cooled to extremely low temperatures, making widespread use costly and complicated.

Now, researchers from Utrecht, Leiden, and Munich have uncovered an important clue about how superconductivity might eventually work at room temperature. Their findings, published in the journal Science, reveal that one of the essential requirements for superconductivity can already be satisfied without extreme cooling. The discovery offers a promising new direction in the search for materials that conduct electricity without resistance.

To understand why this matters, consider something as ordinary as a toaster. When electricity passes through its metal heating element, electrical resistance causes the wire to heat up and glow red, producing the heat needed to toast bread.

That resistance is useful for cooking, but in most electrical systems, it creates unwanted energy losses. Even something as simple as charging a phone involves some electricity being converted into heat rather than being put to useful work.

Why Superconductivity Requires Extreme Cold

Superconductivity eliminates this problem by allowing electrical current to move through certain materials with zero resistance. In principle, this could dramatically improve the efficiency of electrical systems and enable technologies that are difficult or expensive to operate today.

The challenge is temperature. Many superconductors must be cooled to approximately -260°C using liquid helium before they exhibit this remarkable behavior. Maintaining such extreme conditions requires substantial energy and expensive cooling equipment, limiting practical applications.

Superconductivity was first observed in 1911. Decades later, in the mid-1980s, researchers discovered a new class of materials that could become superconducting at much warmer temperatures, around -173°C. Although still extremely cold, this represented an important advance.

However, these materials introduced a major scientific mystery. The established theory that successfully describes conventional, low-temperature superconductivity could not explain how the newer materials worked. Despite decades of research, the mechanisms behind high-temperature superconductivity remain poorly understood.

"We don't understand superconductivity at these higher temperatures at all," says Ingmar Swart [LINK], one of the research leaders. "And if you don't understand it, you can't systematically search for materials that become superconducting at room temperature, which is ultimately our goal."

A Crucial Ingredient Works at Room Temperature

The new study provides an important piece of the puzzle. Swart and his colleagues have demonstrated that one of the two fundamental conditions needed for superconductivity can exist even at room temperature.

"This is really good news," says Swart. "We show that one of the two key conditions for superconductivity can be met at room temperature. If that weren't possible, room-temperature superconductivity would be out of reach altogether."

The finding suggests that scientists may need to focus less on whether electrons can form the necessary connections and more on how those electrons coordinate their behavior.

The Secret Lies in How Electrons Move Together

Superconductivity depends on two essential processes. First, electrons must join together in pairs called Cooper pairs. Second, those pairs must move in a coordinated way, maintaining a shared quantum state that allows electrical current to flow without resistance.

An analogy is a dance floor filled with ten couples. Having each couple dance together is only the first step. For the entire group to move as one, all ten couples must also coordinate their movements.

In conventional superconductors, electron pairing and this collective coordination emerge at the same temperature. The new findings show that high-temperature superconductors behave differently. Their electrons can form pairs at temperatures substantially higher than those needed for superconductivity itself to appear.

Even more remarkably, the researchers found that these pairs can remain intact at room temperature.

"The 'glue' that holds the pairs together is strong enough to keep them together even at room temperature," says Swart. "This suggests that the second key ingredient, phase coherence, is the bottleneck."

Phase coherence describes the coordinated quantum behavior of the electron pairs. Without it, the pairs may exist, but the material does not become superconducting. This suggests that achieving and maintaining that coordination could be the crucial remaining challenge.

"If we understand phase coherence, it may point to a path toward superconductivity at higher temperatures."

Swart intends to investigate this process in future research, with the goal of understanding how superconductivity might be sustained at increasingly warmer temperatures.

New Technology Reveals a Hidden Superconductivity Clue

The breakthrough was made possible by specialized measurement equipment designed and constructed by the research team.

Unlike conventional measurement approaches, the new instruments could distinguish electrical current flowing through individual electrons from current carried by paired electrons. This allowed the researchers to examine when electron pairs formed and how they behaved inside the material.

By separating these two contributions, the team gained a clearer picture of the processes underlying high-temperature superconductivity and identified where a critical obstacle may lie.

The findings do not mean that room-temperature superconductivity has been achieved. They do, however, demonstrate that one of its essential ingredients can survive under everyday temperature conditions. Understanding how to make those electron pairs act together could bring scientists closer to a long-sought breakthrough in electrical technology.

Materials provided by Utrecht University, Faculty of Science. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#603. ‘Love Island’ Winner Bryce Alakai Is Going All-In on His Music Career

Back with a new single "Conscience," the musician says the release reminds him of someone special: "I like the lyrics because it always reminds me of Trinity — fall in love with your best friend."

No one can accuse Bryce Alakai of not being dedicated to craft. The 30-year-old, who broke out as the winner of Love Island alongside his now-girlfriend Trinity Tatum, has been steadily growing his profile as a music producer and DJ in the wake of the show. While it’s common for reality stars to pivot in another field after their breakthrough moment, Alakai has been hustling in the space long before the dating competition series.

When the FAA issued a ground stop on Nov. 13, halting all flights around the country, Alakai found himself in a bit of a pickle. He had four shows back-to-back that weekend. Thankfully, he’d made it from Toronto to Atlanta, but that’s where things got tricky. The flights from Atlanta to Florida were canceled, so instead of canceling the shows, like others might’ve, he got in a car and drove about eight hours to his Florida shows. Related Stories Music Taylor Swift Performs "Our Song" and "I Knew It, I Knew You" at the CMAs TV Where to Watch the 2026 CMA Awards, Featuring Taylor Swift's Return to the Stage

Alakai and Tatum were fan favorites, eventually winning the show’s eighth season earlier this year. Tatum remains his biggest cheerleader, and the feeling is mutual. “It’s just cool because we’re doing different lanes. She’s so deep in fashion. She’s enveloped in that world. I’m obviously maxed out in music right now,” he tells The Hollywood Reporter on a Zoom. “We’re supporting each other’s dreams.”

With a new single “Conscience,” released on Nov. 20 through Ultra Records, Alakai is going all-in on his career as a musician. “I wanted my first release with Ultra to be just a very happy song, very upbeat,” he says.

“I like the lyrics because it always reminds me of Trinity — fall in love with your best friend,” he says. “The whole point of [the song] is just got to live your life, make your mistakes, do what you got to do — but also just enjoy the ride.”

Below, Alakai speaks with THR about producing, balancing his relationship with post-Love Island fame and his new single.

Have the last few months been just nonstop for you?

It’s been literally the definition of zero to 100.

Were you anticipating that or hoping for that?

No. I was 29, turning 30. I was in that place in my life, where it’d be nice to have a person. … I always thought if something comes from it outside of that, that’d be great. But I didn’t think it would be to the extent that it is. I thought it’d be pretty minor. Oh, you got a deal here or there and then you move on with your life. This has been crazy. But I have such a good team that just took the little fire and fanned the shit out of it.

Are you hearing from people after your sets? Are they excited?

It’s insane to be honest. I was in Toronto for that show [I’d mentioned]. Even the venue told me it was the fastest-selling show they’d ever had there. I was so excited to be there because it was such a big crowd. It was like 2,500 people. They’re all hard tickets. Dude, when I walked out, everyone was just screaming. It was crazy. I get the adrenaline. I probably shouldn’t do this, but I check a lot of what people have said after the show because I’m just curious. I’m always trying to see how people are receiving what we’re doing, and 99 percent is all positive. That makes me feel good. I had a girl send me a message the other night [that] said it was the best night she’s ever had in her life. I was reading it, I was like, “That’s insane.” Obviously those things are pretty validating, but I feel like the overall response has been really positive.

This is obviously something you were doing before Love Island, but have you felt people question if you’re taking it seriously in the wake of the show?

Oh, 100 percent. Thankfully I had all my stuff on TikTok already posted up from the past years, so there’s obviously videos of me DJing. Three weeks before I went to Fiji, I opened for Carlita and John Summit, which was my biggest show to date. I was already getting a little traction with it. We were starting to make some moves. When I got off [of Love Island] I saw that everyone kind of recognized [I’d been doing it], so it created a different … I think that’s why maybe the shows have been doing so well, there was already that layer before. At first, the first show, I think people were questioning if I could do it. “Just because he did it before doesn’t mean he is actually good.” After each one of these shows, the credibility has slowly gone up. Now, we’re releasing this new song on Nov. 20 with Ultra. I just feel like I’ve gotten a lot of industry backing that is pretty rare from something like this. The collab interests that I’ve been getting, and the sessions I’ve been doing have been in — it’s been insane. I always feel like I’m in a dream because I feel like with any other career, you see the progression in front of you. With this, it was literally just zero to full on go mode, which I’m really grateful for. It is surreal just because it’s like you’re just jumping straight in.

There’s not much downtime these days, right? You’re also starting this new life with another person, so that’s an added element as well.

That definitely adds a layer to it. I’ve been with her today. We had just flew back last night, I’m with her today and then I have to fly to Vegas tomorrow. Thankfully, she’s coming to Vegas too a couple days later, but it really makes it so I have to check in with her and balance the time. It’s just hard because with these dates, I want to be my best at these performances, but I also don’t want to neglect her and make her ever feel like she’s not my priority because she is. It’s just a balancing game I’ve been learning that I haven’t had to do before and to make sure I water both aspects of my life equally.

Today, I have two sessions after this call and then she has an interview and then another thing and then shooting a video. We come back at night. All this shit just happened. It’s just a balancing thing on both of us, and we’re figuring it out. But with how busy we both are, it definitely doesn’t make it easier. I think our communication is so good that we figure it out.

#602. More than a billion years of Earth's history vanished. Scientists may finally know why

More than a billion years of Earth's geological history are missing from some of the planet's rock formations. Scientists have debated the cause of this enormous gap for decades, but new research suggests that the answer may lie in the slow movement of entire continents, driven by powerful forces deep inside Earth.

A study led by a PhD candidate at the University of Wollongong (UOW) offers a new explanation for the Great Unconformity, one of geology's most enduring mysteries. Published in the journal Nature, the findings suggest that ancient continents gradually rose and sank over hundreds of millions of years as hot rock moved through Earth's interior. These changes in elevation may have allowed erosion to remove enormous amounts of rock, erasing vast stretches of the planet's geological record.

Lead author Santosh Dhungana, a UOW PhD candidate, explained that although researchers have proposed numerous explanations for the Great Unconformity, few have been rigorously tested against the long-term behavior of Earth's interior.

"Imagine a book where a huge section in the middle has been ripped out. The Great Unconformity is that gap in Earth's story, with the narrative jumping from the early chapters straight to a much later part of the story. Our research suggests these pages weren't lost by chance," he said.

Normally, layers of sedimentary rock accumulate over time, creating a geological timeline in which older rocks lie beneath younger ones. Scientists can study these layers to reconstruct ancient environments and understand how Earth has changed over billions of years.

Yet this timeline contains a remarkable interruption. At numerous locations worldwide, sedimentary rocks dating to the Cambrian period, around 540 million years ago, rest directly on much older crystalline rocks, including granite that can be more than a billion years old. The intervening geological layers are absent, leaving an enormous break in the record known as the Great Unconformity.

One of the clearest examples is visible in the Grand Canyon in the United States. This region was once part of Laurentia (modern North America), an ancient continental landmass. Similar gaps have been identified in Europe, Australia, Africa and Asia.

The amount of missing time varies considerably between locations. In some places, approximately 200 million years of geological history are absent, while elsewhere the gap exceeds a billion years.

How Forces Deep Inside Earth May Have Erased the Rock Record

To investigate what caused these missing chapters, Dhungana worked with his supervisor and co-author, Associate Professor Nicolas Flament, to simulate the movement of Earth's mantle over hundreds of millions of years.

The mantle is an immense layer of hot, mostly solid rock beneath Earth's crust. Although this material appears rigid on human timescales, it can deform and flow extremely slowly over geological periods. Heat-driven circulation within the mantle, a process called mantle convection, can gradually raise enormous regions of Earth's surface or cause them to subside.

These vertical movements can influence whether ancient rocks are exposed to erosion or buried beneath new deposits. When a continent rises, wind, water and other natural processes can gradually wear away its surface. If the land later sinks, oceans can advance over it, allowing fresh sediment to accumulate on top of the eroded rock.

The researchers found that this process may explain both the disappearance of ancient rock layers and the preservation of the geological boundary that remains visible today.

Ancient Continents Rose and Sank Over Millions of Years

The simulations revealed a striking pattern across three major ancient continental regions: Laurentia, Baltica (northern Europe) and North China.

According to the models, mantle convection caused the ancient cores of these continents to rise during the Neoproterozoic Era, which extended from roughly one billion to 540 million years ago. This long interval preceded the Cambrian period, when animal life underwent a remarkable expansion in diversity, commonly known as the Cambrian explosion.

As the continents remained elevated, prolonged erosion could have stripped away extensive layers of older rock, gradually removing hundreds of millions of years of geological history.

The researchers found that this period of uplift was followed by widespread subsidence during the Phanerozoic eon, which encompasses approximately the past 540 million years. As these ancient continental regions slowly sank, advancing seas covered their eroded surfaces. New sediments accumulated above the exposed older rocks, preserving the boundary between the two.

Over immense spans of time, this sequence of uplift, erosion, subsidence and sediment deposition could have produced the Great Unconformity seen in rock formations today.

A New Explanation for One of Earth's Greatest Geological Mysteries

A particularly important finding was how closely the computer simulations matched the geographical distribution of the Great Unconformity.

The models predicted long-term uplift followed by subsidence in North America, northern Europe and North China, precisely the regions where the geological gap is especially well documented and preserved.

This agreement provides support for the idea that deep mantle movements played a major role in shaping the missing rock record. Rather than requiring a separate explanation for each location, the findings suggest that a common process operating deep within Earth may account for the widespread pattern.

"Sometimes what is missing can tell us more about the story of Earth than what we can see. A single, long period of uplift followed by a long period of sinking would have been the ideal recipe for removing the rock and preserving the worn surface," Associate Professor Flament said.

The research offers a way to connect the geological evidence visible at Earth's surface with the slow processes occurring far below it. Although the findings do not establish that mantle convection was the only factor responsible for the Great Unconformity, they provide a testable explanation for why so much ancient geological history disappeared and how the remaining evidence survived.

"Many explanations for the Great Unconformity had been proposed but few had been tested against how the Earth actually behaves over time. It is a thrill to be able to propose a solution to this geological puzzle."

Materials provided by University of Wollongong. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
